DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.

items.title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
items.author: JB Kim, Byungwoo Jeon, Kyungmin Lee
items.text: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

items.title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
items.author: Ruixiang Wang, Xinyue Yao, Xuanning Zhou
items.text: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

items.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
items.author: Bohe Chen
items.text: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

items.title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
items.author: Xiang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Ya-Li Li
items.text: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at

items.title: Change the Base, Change the Game: Rethinking Pan-sharpening
items.author: Jeonghyeok Do, Geunhyuk Youk, Munchurl Kim
items.text: Many pan-sharpening (PS) networks reconstruct high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) images by adding learned residuals to 4times-interpolated low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) inputs, incorporating panchromatic (PAN) detail only through these residual corrections. This raises a simple question: Why start with a blurry base when sharp spatial detail is already available? We propose PanBase, a sharper multispectral starting point designed for more effective residual learning. Guided by physical sensor characteristics, PanBase combines PAN spatial detail with LRMS spectral information while enforcing consistency with the LRMS observations under sensor-specific blur. We construct this base without neural network training, estimating only nine coefficients per spectral band through closed-form calibration. Our PanBase can be easily integrated into existing backbones with a global residual skip through two simple changes: (i) replacing the skip base with PanBase and (ii) concatenating it as an additional input. Using each backbone's original training recipe and matched training budgets, PanBase improves most reduced- and full-resolution metrics on WorldView-3, QuickBird, and GaoFen-2, while achieving 4.4times faster training convergence on average. In zero-shot evaluation on WorldView-2, standalone PanBase achieves competitive reconstruction without target-sensor fitting or neural refinement.

items.title: Playfulness as Feedback for Agentic Game Development
items.author: Weijia Mao, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Zhen Fang
items.text: Coding agents can generate runnable games from natural-language descriptions. However, a runnable game does not guarantee an excellent gameplay experience for players. In our view, a playful game should provide 1) reliable core functionality, 2) appealing visual design and assets, and 3) rich gameplay that supports exploration and progression. How agents can improve these aspects of playfulness remains underexplored. In our work, we propose Play2Evolve, a recursive game development framework with three stages: Initialization, Refinement, and Evolution. Using playfulness as feedback, agents playtest the game and diagnose issues in its functionality, visual presentation, and gameplay. Their feedback guides bug fixes and asset improvements. It also helps agents propose new gameplay and aesthetic goals for continued game evolution. To enrich game materials, we combine a video generation model with code to create appealing static and dynamic assets and integrate them into interactive gameplay. Finally, Play2Evolve achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods, scoring 60.05 on GameCraft-Bench compared with 50.81 after Game Initialization and 52.46 for Play2Code. Human overall-quality ratings reach 3.67, compared with 2.38 and 2.43, respectively. Our code will be released at

items.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
items.author: Hoang-Nhat Nguyen, Chen Change Loy
items.text: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

items.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
items.author: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang
items.text: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at

items.title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
items.author: Zhiyue Zhao, Mingyu Liu, Bolin Zhang
items.text: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.

items.title: SPARC: Geometry-Guided Attention Pruning for Long-Horizon Camera-Controlled Video Generation
items.author: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui
items.text: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at

items.title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
items.author: Jiachen An, Sijie Zhao, Le Li
items.text: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.

items.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
items.author: Yurun Chen, Biao Yi, Qihang Yu
items.text: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

items.title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
items.author: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu
items.text: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

items.title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
items.author: Baihan Yang, Xin Lin, Yufan Wei
items.text: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page:

items.title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time
items.author: Jianyu Wu, Yizhou Wang, Encheng Su
items.text: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

items.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
items.author: Abhinav Sharma, Li Li, Chien Van Nguyen
items.text: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

items.title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control
items.author: Lisiyu Pan, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang
items.text: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training. At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration. Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code: Website:

items.title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
items.author: Boxuan Dong, Yupeng Qian, Ying Wu
items.text: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at

items.title: SIA: Selective Image Analogy
items.author: Amirhossein Alimohammadi, Kian Izadpanah, Bardiya Kariminia
items.text: Image analogy transfers a demonstrated transformation from a before/after pair (A, A') to a new query image B. Existing methods assume all changes in (A, A') should be fully transferred, limiting flexibility when users want only a subset of the demonstrated edits. We introduce Selective Image Analogy (SIA), a new setting where a single demonstration pair encodes multiple edits, and the user selects at inference time which edits to apply to B. To support this, we curate a multi-edit analogy dataset with full-edit and partial-edit targets. We then train a model that first learns to transfer the complete demonstrated transformation, and then gains selective control through a mask-aligned suppression mechanism: a token-gated LoRA that restricts adapter updates to suppressed edit tokens during denoising, paired with a concept suppression vector that weakens the selected tokens in the text embeddings before denoising. Together, these components allow SIA to suppress unwanted edits that remain visible in A', while preserving the user-selected ones, all without requiring a new demonstration pair for each edit combination. We perform extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations along with user studies to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
items.author: Yongchang Zhang, Jie Huang, Yunhe Ni
items.text: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to N times M integrations when evaluating N methods on M benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.

items.title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos
items.author: Yuchen Zhou, Hongsheng Wu, Jiayu Tang
items.text: Embodied agents operating around people must not only recognize social cues, but also decide when the available evidence is sufficient, whether to intervene, and how to respond without violating social norms. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these abilities in isolation or with access to completed videos, obscuring where an online social decision fails. We introduce AIRIS, a causal streaming benchmark that formulates social embodied intelligence as a time-anchored chain of Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction (A-I-R-I). AIRIS contains 8,000 expert-curated questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips across 11 context categories and 36 capability dimensions. At each query, models receive only the observation prefix available at that time; decision-aware metrics reward calibrated waiting and complete reactions while penalizing premature commitment. Evaluating 45 proprietary and open-source general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal models reveals fragmented and temporally miscalibrated competence. General-purpose VLMs excel at passive cue grounding and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated reaction sub-decisions; yet across all families, models frequently guess intents before sufficient evidence emerges and fail to jointly align intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution within the same episode. AIRIS thus provides a diagnostic foundation for bridging the gap between passive social perception and reliable embodied interaction.

items.title: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos
items.author: Ji Xie, Yanhao Jia, Xiangpeng Yang
items.text: Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.

items.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
items.author: Jiacheng Xu, Shuo He, Fuxiang Zhang
items.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

items.title: RoboEvo^2: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
items.author: Chenzhi Liu, Jiehong Lin, Wei Huang
items.text: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo^2, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo^2 improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

items.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
items.author: Shenxing Wei, Jinxi Li, Zihui Zhang
items.text: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

items.title: 3D CoCa v3: Contrastive Learners with Scene Graphs for Urban Scene Understanding
items.author: Nannan Zhang, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang
items.text: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at

items.title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
items.author: Dongheon Lee, DongJae Lee, Sewhan Chun
items.text: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a 4.24times inference speedup over existing methods.

items.title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
items.author: Med Team, Ming Hu, Cheng Tang
items.text: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

items.title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation
items.author: Xuanyu Zheng, Luoyuan Zhang, Yancheng Long
items.text: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.

items.title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation
items.author: Shaoteng Liu, Shuai Yang, Wei Huang
items.text: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

items.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
items.author: Wenrui Zhou, Jiashun Liu, Sujie Hu
items.text: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

items.title: Loupe: Reinforcing Knowledge-Intensive Video Generation Agents
items.author: Kai Zeng, Ruichuan An, Zhen Fang
items.text: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at

items.title: CONCOR: Benchmarking Contrastive Decoding for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Beyond Final-Output Performance
items.author: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen
items.text: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

items.title: Target-Part Preference Optimization for Part-Aware 3D Generation
items.author: Zishan Qin, Rui Li, Zeyu Zhang
items.text: Part-aware 3D generation requires not only globally plausible objects but also complete, well-separated semantic parts, yet high-quality part decompositions remain too scarce to support large-scale supervised fine-tuning. We study whether preference fine-tuning based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) can adapt a pretrained part-aware generator from limited part-annotated data without architectural changes. We rank candidates generated with different random seeds against ground-truth (GT) geometric metrics, and select the (object, target-part) examples with the largest across-seed quality gap. Each selected example stores a seed pair whose two flow trajectories share one clean GT compositional latent and differ only in Gaussian noise. We derive a reference-relative target-block preference loss from FlowDPO that compares the two trajectories against a frozen reference model. GT flow-matching losses on the target block and complete part set provide absolute supervision, while only the diffusion transformer (DiT) is updated. Human-ranked controls test an alternative ordering source, and synthetic cropping provides controlled loser targets that are incomplete by construction. Among the three training-set scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest result on held-out Objaverse and outperforms both the pretrained generator and the reported direct supervised fine-tuning baseline on the multi-part aggregate. Further analysis shows sensitivity to pair ordering, target-part coverage, and the balance between pairwise and GT supervision. Cross-dataset experiments show less consistent gains under distribution shift.

items.title: Show HN: Graphvein – Trace calls to handlers and tables across repos, no LLM
items.author: saptashwa
items.text: As I started developing more projects using AI assistance over this year, I started facing the problem that most people have voiced against using AI - the overall architecture/design of the project becomes known only to the agent, and you lose control of the project. I thought what if we could map the architecture, calls, routes, table schemas etc. from the code - that is how this project was born in October. Now I searched a little bit and came upon a few different projects, but none of them did what I wanted to do - at least in full. And quite a few of them used LLMs themselves to do that - which could be plausibly wrong (hallucinated) and non deterministic. Therefore I have built this over the last 2 months to create a base which: 1. Extracts routes, table schema, request and response bodies across HTTP requests, Tauri calls etc. 2. Gives you an overview of the architecture which you can dive into including how each handler is linked to routes or tables - it works in both directions in a fan out mode from any layer 3. Gives you an overview of the table schema extracted from the project and how they link together 4. An OpenAPI spec extracted from the project, with a try-it mode like Swagger 5. Change impact and what changing a particular piece of code might impact across the stack 6. It supports zero or more frontends, and one or more backends together in a project and how they all link together It supports TypeScript / JavaScript (Express, Next.js, Angular, Angular HttpClient, hey-api, fetch, axios, Prisma, Drizzle, Sequelize, TypeORM, Orval and Supabase clients), Python (FastAPI, SQLModel), Go (net/http, chi, gin, GORM), and Rust (Axum, Tauri commands, Diesel). Database support is for SQL (tested with Postgres) and Java, C# and Dart get structure only in this preview release. It also has a read-only MCP server which agents can use to get Graphvein-verified information and not have to grep around files to figure things out. No data leaves your computer (other than the try it environments you configure yourself), and everything is done locally, without any LLM (not even local LLMs). I do plan on adding LLM support in the future, but only building upon this base - for gap-filling, generation of wikis and other features which can use the deterministic core and build upon it. And it will remain opt-in even then. Please feel free to check out the GitHub repo or the website ( to get more details. Please let me know which language support/framework would make this more appealing to use, or if you have any other feature requests.

items.title: Show HN: Neui – Go web apps with a built-in AI agent
items.author: derstruct
items.text:
Neui is an AI agent and a web framework built as one stack. The core is a server-driven Go web framework ( neui ( turns each page into an agent harness. FEATURES: The agent sees & operates UI. Annotate what agent can access (links, inputs, buttons), so agent sees it and can assist user with UI operations or even automate it with scripting. ~>neui.Use{ Desc:"submit the form" } or expose context data for the agent:
~neui.Data{Text: "the product shown in the card", Object: product} ...
Dynamic tools, right in the markup Same way as you render a button to the user, you give the agent a tool. No endpoints or lifecycle management needed. ~(if user.IsAdmin() { ~neui.Tool[Refund, Receipt]{ Name: "refund", Desc: "Refund the order", Handler: orders.Refund, } }) Work environment Isolated file workspaces and sandboxed scripting ("code mode") out of the box. Agentic apps When a user needs something your UI doesn't have, agent builds it on demand. Complete chat experience Thread list, history, message edits, full-text search, a message queue and automatic compaction. Batteries included MCP connector, web search and .xlsx tools, rich building blocks library for generative apps. COMPARED TO COPILOT KIT: - Agent thread runs on the server, so browser can't rewrite the history/tools to use your LLM backend + less traffic and faster tool-loops - System prompt and provided tool list do not change during operation - it caches and stays hot (because it's usually the same for all your users!) - Pull-based, targeted UI sync; agent monitors only parts of UI that are relevant to the task (compared to full state attached to any user message) - Neui is already a harness with its own sandbox - just bring your model. - For generative UI agent writes a small app on specialized micro framework; agent doesn't need to answer each click or load user input/API responses into context - CON: Is not stack-agnostic, like AG-UI stuff TRY IT: The repo has a demo app with all of this: git clone && cd neui DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=... go run ./examples/business-systems/backoffice Then open Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek and any OpenAI-compatible provider will work. STATUS: Both doors and neui are Apache-2.0. I released the first version about 3 weeks ago, so it's early and I am still optimizing some system instructions. Neui itself took me 3 months, on top of the 2 years I spent on the framework underneath (it's awesome, btw), which made it possible.

items.title: BCDD: A small contract language for telling an LLM what a system must do
items.author: PaoloGe
items.text: 1.0-beta BCDD (Behavioural Contract-Driven Design) è un linguaggio per specificare il comportamento di un sistema attraverso i suoi confini con l'esterno. Una CSC (Capability State Contract) è un contratto su ciò che si può chiedere a un'entità e su ciò che di essa si può vedere. bcdd è il programma che controlla i file CSC. Un tentativo di nuovo paradigma per un uso serio dell'intelligenza artificiale (IA) nella progettazione Nell'uso quotidiano dell'IA per ottenere risultati concreti mi sono apparse evidenti due cose. Dialogare con l'IA è facile; è difficile, invece, sintetizzare per un obiettivo preciso tutte le specifiche e i requisiti che definiscono il risultato voluto. Anche la descrizione di dettaglio è insidiosa: si tende a semplificare e a tacere ciò che l'esperienza fa ritenere ovvio, ma ciò che è ovvio per chi chiede non lo è per chi esegue. L'IA segna un salto nella produzione del software: il lavoro si sposta dall'implementazione alla progettazione di scatole nere funzionali, di cui vanno descritti compiutamente il comportamento e gli stati. Nel BCDD questa descrizione prende la forma delle CSC. La stessa IA può aiutare a scrivere e a completare le CSC di un'entità la cui implementazione sarà poi affidata all'IA stessa, indipendentemente dall'ambiente di sviluppo, dal sistema operativo e dal linguaggio di programmazione. Il paradigma è applicabile anche ad altri campi, a sistemi complessi, all'hardware e ai sistemi che uniscono hardware e software. Italiano → BCDD (Behavioural Contract-Driven Design) is a language for specifying the behaviour of a system through its boundaries with the outside. A CSC (Capability State Contract) is a contract on what can be requested of an entity and on what can be seen of it. bcdd is the program that checks CSC files. An attempt at a new paradigm for serious use of artificial intelligence (AI) in design In everyday use of AI to obtain concrete results, two things became clear to me. Conversing with AI is easy; what is hard is to pull together, for a specific goal, all the specifications and requirements that define the intended result. A detailed description is deceptively hard as well: people tend to simplify and to leave unsaid whatever experience makes them consider obvious, but what is obvious to the person making the request is not obvious to whoever carries it out. AI marks a step change in the production of software: the work shifts from implementation to the design of functional black boxes, whose behaviour and states must be described in full. In BCDD this description takes the form of CSCs. The same AI can help write and complete the CSCs of an entity whose implementation will then be handed to AI itself, regardless of the development environment, operating system and programming language. The paradigm also applies to other fields, to complex systems, to hardware and to systems that combine hardware and software. English → Dati dei visitatori (GDPR). Questo è un sito statico: non usa cookie, moduli o statistiche e non carica risorse da servizi di terzi. Il sito è ospitato su un server virtuale (VPS) di IONOS SE, in centri dati nell'Unione europea; IONOS tratta i dati per conto del titolare, come responsabile del trattamento (art. 28 del GDPR). Per ogni visita il server registra in un log tecnico l'indirizzo IP, che è un dato personale, la data e l'ora, la richiesta (metodo, pagina e protocollo), il codice di risposta, i byte trasferiti, la pagina di provenienza e il tipo di browser (User-Agent). Le richieste rifiutate o in errore sono registrate anche in un log degli errori. Il log serve al funzionamento e alla sicurezza del sito (base giuridica: legittimo interesse, art. 6, par. 1, lett. f, del Regolamento UE 2016/679, «GDPR»); i dati sono conservati fino a 15 giorni e poi cancellati. Il titolare del trattamento è Noli Paolo. Per esercitare i diritti previsti dal GDPR (accesso ai propri dati, cancellazione e gli altri) e per qualsiasi altra richiesta: . È sempre…

items.title: LLM Position Bias: Does Naming an Option First Change an AI's Answer?
items.author: ritzaco
items.text: Since the beginning of time, LLMs have always just agreed with their users. In a comparison where an LLM didn't know what to agree with, it would just choose the first-named option, assuming it was the first one that came to the user's mind for a reason. The reason is far less complex than that. Researchers call it position bias, and we wanted to know how much of it today's AI agents still have. We asked Claude Code to choose between 100 pairs of options, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, Slack or Microsoft Teams, McDonald's or Burger King, and heads or tails, 10 times with each option named first. In 72 of the 100 pairs, the agent gave the same answer in all 20 runs, whatever the order. But when it had no real favourite, the order decided the answer. On a coin toss, it called whichever side we named first 19 times out of 20. (Yes, that means you can rig the coin toss when Claude picks who pays for lunch. No, you shouldn't.) This article covers which pairs the order moved, the statistics behind the result, and how to check whether the order is deciding an answer you get from an agent. How we tested All 2,000 sessions used Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) in Claude Code 2.1.326, on 25 and 26 November 2026. Each run was a fresh session in an empty folder, under a clean Claude Code profile with no tools, MCP servers, plugins or memory. Every prompt had the same shape: one sentence of context, then "Should I go with A or B? End your answer with one line: PICK: <name>." The two orders used the same context sentence, so the only difference was which name came first. We ran the 2,000 sessions in a shuffled order so time of day couldn't line up with the order of the names, and we fixed the hypotheses and tests below before the first run. The option named first won 1,031 of the 2,000 runs, or 51.6%. If the order made no difference, you'd expect about 50%. That 1.6-point gap passes a significance test, but only just, and it comes almost entirely from pairs where the agent had no real preference. When it did have a preference, which was most of the time, swapping the order changed nothing. Each dot below is a pair, placed by how often its first option won in each order. If the order made no difference, every dot would sit on the dashed line. The agent gave the same answer in all 20 runs on 61 of the 80 commercial questions, no matter how we asked. It picked PostgreSQL over MySQL for a new SaaS app, Slack over Microsoft Teams for a 50-person company, Toyota over Honda for a reliable family car and Coca-Cola over Pepsi for a party, in all 20 runs each time. Swapping the names round didn't move any of them. The pairs that moved were the ones where the agent's view was already split, which is why non-commercial questions with no clear answer, like tea or coffee, moved most often. Where position bias shows up: when the AI has no favourite The pairs below show what happens when the agent has no settled view of its own. A coin toss is the purest test, because there's no right answer to know. All 20 answers said the call was 50/50, yet the agent picked whichever side we'd named first in 19 of them. Its reasons changed with the order. Asked "Heads or Tails?", it picked heads as "the classic", and asked "Tails or Heads?", it picked tails for a different reason: RequestI'm calling a coin toss to decide who goes first in a game. Should I go with Tails or Heads? Response It's a 50/50 either way … People call heads more often, so tails is a fine contrarian choice. With heads named first, the same question got "I'll go with the classic. PICK: Heads". Both reasons sound sensible, but the order of the names decided the pick, and the agent found a reason for whichever side came first. This was the one commercial pair where the effect was strong enough to count on its own. We said we needed "a message broker for event processing between services", which is a real toss-up: Kafka suits replayable event streams, RabbitMQ suits simpler message passing, and our…

items.title: Show HN: Kestrom – Byte-verifiable LLM edits, IFC decoding, and backdoor scans
items.author: rizumita
items.text: Edit a language model inside a range, and let anyone check, byte for byte, what changed and what did not. Fine-tuning, LoRA, merging and quantization can move the output at any position. After such an edit, the only way to know that "nothing else changed" is to evaluate everything again, and even then you only know it for the prompts you tried. In our runs on Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3-8B, a 4-bit quantization and a public fine-tuned derivative each left 0 of 150 greedy answers the same as the original's. Kestrom takes the other side. Each edit comes with a range that is read from the weights or from the decoding, not from what the editor claims, and a report that anyone can rebuild on their own machine and compare with cmp. original weights ──edit──▶ edited weights ──kestrom-verify──▶ report.json │ W every byte the same but the changed rows │ U0 the original equal to itself on this machine │ G1 every logit outside the range equal, bit for bit (row edits) │ G2 greedy output the same until the range is reached ▼ the receiver rebuilds report.json ─▶ same bytes Two packages: The checks that pass say which tier an edit is in. Kestrom does not blur them. Determinism (U0: the original model gives the same logits and the same greedy output twice on your machine) is checked by logits and measure, which run the original twice, and by compare, on the two outputs of the original you give it. If U0 fails, G1 and G2 in that report mean nothing. range and diff read only bytes. compare checks the output files you give it: write them yourself, running the original twice. For decode-time edits it checks the output against the events the decoding records, not that a loop or a condition was really there. Product scope: - Supported (enterprise evaluation / audit): kestrom-verify (Apache-2.0), kestrom audit, kestrom inspect (including mirror and disarm), kestrom ifc (control / firewall), kestrom kv + kestrom generate --rules (open, loopguard, phrase, add, ban), kestrom rules (fit, run, build, weigh), kestrom steer, kestrom rows ban-row / ban, and kestrom bridge. - Experimental (research / reproduction): kestrom edit, kestrom trigger, kestrom find, kestrom rows lsq / ftpo, kestrom rules write-mlp, kestrom train sft-data, and kestrom merge. Every tool is in, whether or not it reached the target we set for it. The table gives the tier and what we measured, with the target where one was missed. A tool's guarantee says what did not change; whether the edit does what you want is measured, and for several tools it fell short. Each command's help (kestrom, kestrom <command> --help, python -m pydoc kestrom.<module>) has the details. The decode-time edits are all written in one rules language (python -m pydoc kestrom.rules) and combine freely. For example, plain style for free-form questions only, no Chinese tokens in the answer after thinking, no **, and the loop guard: in free: prompt style.npz 16 # a condition read on the prompt (kestrom steer direction) in think: thinking h1 f: all(free) h1 answer: all(!think) h2 plain: all(f) h2 ans: all(answer) add style.npz 16: 14.6*plain # conditional steering ban 的 了 们: ans # these tokens never, once thinking is over phrase: "**" # go back and avoid it loopguard: 512 kestrom generate MODEL prompts.json out.jsonl --rules edit.dsl records the events of every line, and kestrom-verify compare events checks that each output is the original's until its first event. Rules that read probed features of the hidden state are fitted first (kestrom rules fit, optionally at a decoder LAYER >= 0 so kestrom bridge rules can transfer FIT.npz across models). An open line connects rules written with no model to a model's answer: open meter: router.dsl ask runs the rules of router.dsl (a network of their own, below) on each prompt's data and makes the output open with the class their head meter answers and a line feed, or with ask where they answer none (without the last word, nothing is done there). Where the model's own top tokens…

items.title: Show HN: Selenia – Plain-English Selenium locators from a 24 MB model, no LLM
items.author: penielny
items.text: Stop maintaining brittle XPath. Find Selenium elements with plain English, using a 24 MB model that runs locally. No LLM, no API key, no per-call cost. A real run: every element is chosen by the model from the page's own elements. Locators break whenever the front end changes: a renamed class, a moved div, a regenerated id. LLM browser agents can avoid that, but they need an API key, send your pages to a third party, cost money on every step, take seconds per action, and can confidently pick the wrong element. Selenia does one job: it turns a description into an element. A small fine-tuned ranking model scores the real elements on the page against your description and returns the best one. It never writes a selector, so it cannot invent one. If you want an autonomous agent, use an agent. If you want reliable, fast, free locators inside the Selenium tests you already have, use Selenia. pip install selenia Or from source: pip install .from selenium import webdriver from selenia import Selenia driver = webdriver.Chrome() selenia = Selenia(driver) # downloads the model on first use driver.get(" selenia.find("username field").send_keys("standard_user") selenia.find("password field").send_keys("secret_sauce") selenia.find("the login button").click() # Find all matching elements, best match first buttons = selenia.find_all("add to cart button") find returns a normal Selenium WebElement, so it works alongside your existing code, waits and page objects. Elements inside open shadow DOM are found too. More runnable scripts, including a full checkout flow, error handling and a pytest suite, are in examples/. - find raises Selenium's NoSuchElementException when the model is not confident (min_score, default 0.5) or when two elements fit equally well (min_margin, default 0.05). The message names the candidates, so you can see what to add to the description. - find_all returns every element scoring at least min_score, best first. - Tune both with LocalRanker(min_score=..., min_margin=...); min_margin=0 always takes the top pick. - iframes are not searched: switch into the frame first, then call find. A cross-encoder (based on ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2) fine-tuned on about 28,800 description/element pairs collected from real websites, then exported to int8 ONNX. It runs on onnxruntime and tokenizers, so there is no PyTorch dependency. The first time you create a Selenia, it downloads the model (about 24 MB) into ~/.cache/selenia and verifies its checksum. After that it runs offline. - SELENIA_CACHE_DIR changes where the download is kept. - SELENIA_MODEL_URL fetches from your own mirror instead of the GitHub release. - To use a model you trained yourself, pass LocalRanker(model_dir="training/models/selenia-ce") or set SELENIA_MODEL_DIR. That is the folder written by training/train.py. The full pipeline that produced the model (collecting pages, labelling, generating descriptions, fine-tuning, int8 export and evaluation) is in training/. Retraining on screens from your own product is the fastest way to push accuracy higher for your tests. python -m pytest tests/ The tests in tests/test_browser.py drive a headless Chrome against a local page and are skipped when Chrome cannot start. The ones that use the real model are also skipped unless a trained model is at training/models/selenia-ce or SELENIA_MODEL_DIR. Issues and pull requests are welcome. Especially useful: pages where Selenia picks the wrong element (open an issue with the URL and your description), so they can be added to the training and evaluation data. If Selenia saves you from fixing a broken locator, a ⭐ helps other people find it. Made with ❤️ by Penielny
