items.title: The state of LLM: costs and capabilities
items.author: krsaulitis
items.text: Between 9 and 18 November, Anthropic, Google and OpenAI released six flagship and mid-tier models between them. Every launch post claimed some benchmark crown, and after a while we stopped being able to tell which of it mattered for us. So instead of following the launches, we went back to the people who measure this stuff for a living: Epoch AI, METR, Stanford's AI Index team, economists running randomized trials, and Artificial Analysis, which is honestly the site our team opens most often when picking a model. We wanted answers to a few practical questions. How fast are LLMs actually getting cheaper, and why isn't our bill shrinking? What can the models do now that they couldn't a year ago? Who's making money? Does any of it make people more productive? And is it worth running models on our own hardware, rented or bought? Building a product on LLMs is a bet that prices, capabilities and reliability keep moving in the right direction. The last section is my own guess at how that bet plays out, and it's labelled as such. LLMs became "AI" in under four years ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022, so it isn't even four years old. In that short time, LLMs have more or less taken over the word "AI". In February 2026 Pew asked 5,119 Americans, for the first time, which technology comes to mind first when they think of AI. 29% named chatbots, either in general or a brand like ChatGPT, and another 6% said generative AI or LLMs. Robots and science fiction got 8%. In the same survey, the share of Americans who had heard "a lot" about AI rose from 26% in 2022 to 48%. ChatGPT alone passed a billion weekly users in August 2026, and Google's Gemini passed a billion monthly users around the same time. That matters for this post because the word hides a lot. Speech recognition, computer vision, recommendation systems and plain old machine learning are AI too, and they work under very different economics. We feel this every day. Asya is an AI company, but most of what our developers build are new models that aren't LLMs at all. When someone hears "AI company" and assumes we wrap ChatGPT, it's a good reminder of how much the word has narrowed. The costs, capabilities and risks we look at here belong to large language models specifically, so in this post we say LLMs when we mean LLMs. The exceptions are proper names (Epoch AI, the AI Index, the EU AI Act) and places where we quote a survey that asked about "AI" in general. LLMs are getting cheaper faster than any technology before them The best long-run data comes from Epoch AI. In September it published The plunging price of thought, which tracks what it costs to hit a fixed score on five benchmarks (GPQA Diamond and FrontierMath among them). Since 2023 that cost has dropped about 47% a quarter, which works out to roughly 13× a year. Epoch compared it with other technologies, and the result is a bit absurd: about 4× faster than the fall in DNA sequencing costs, 6× faster than compute, 18× faster than lithium-ion batteries and 54× faster than electricity between 1892 and 1973. The top example in the chart is my favourite from the report. GPQA Diamond is a set of PhD-level science questions, and getting 75% of them right went from about 30 cents a question to well under a tenth of a cent in less than 18 months. The bottom example is the one a16z called "LLMflation" back in 2024. Other studies land in the same place. Mingdeng Du at Wuhan University combined OpenRouter data on 318 models with Epoch's records of 3,237 and found token prices fell about 600-fold, from GPT-3's $60 per million tokens in 2020 to $0.10 for economy-tier models in early 2026. An earlier Epoch study found the rate varies a lot depending on which milestone you pick, anywhere from 9× to 900× a year. One caveat, which Epoch raises itself: all of this rests on benchmarks. Models can be trained to the test, benchmark questions aren't real work, and the calculation assumes you always switch to the cheapest model that can do the…

items.title: What LLMs Do to PostgreSQL and DBAs
items.author: 0x54MUR41
items.text: Recently there has been some discussion about why so many features got reverted from PostgreSQL 19. I've read blogposts, talked with people, spent some time thinking. And it got me curious. I noticed lately that there is more mails to pgsql-bugs mailing list – basically reports of bugs, or conversations about them. I also noticed that there are fewer emails to pgsql-general. So figured I'll try to gather some stats, and maybe even put them in form of charts. First, to give some perspective pgsql-hackers – very busy list: As you can see there is data since beginning of 2024, so almost 3 years. And I do see some uptick recently in number of new threads (yellow line), but total number of emails per week is somewhat stable. Bug reports though look different: Reports of new bugs went up sometime between May and September. We can see it better zooming on 2026 only: And this shows non trivial increase since mid-July. And finally pgsql-general: and zoom in to 2026: Personally, I “blame" LLMs. They made more people research (and find) bugs. Which caused spike in number of mails to -bugs. But they also are used by a lot of people to answer questions. So now, there are WAY fewer mails to -general. Incidentally this also matches that I see Slack and Discord – discussions there are almost gone. Why ask there, take a chance that someone might be unpleasant, or maybe even noone will answer, when you can get good (enough) answer in 5 minutes from some random LLM. Interestingly, while traffic on IRC, did drop too (from average 5900 messages per month in 2024, to ~ 3200 per month in 2025, and recently to ~ 700 per month), I think that it is more active than discord and slack, which note couple of messages per week. At most. Life of DBAs has changed. Apparently we now prefer to ask robots instead of fellow people. Whether it's good or bad, or if it even should be qualified in this way – it's up to you to decide. On my final note I can only say that traffic to explain.depesz.com dropped significantly, and while I think that some of this drop was people moving to other visualizers, perhaps explain.dalibo.com, I kinda think/know/assume, that most of the drop is simply people trusting machines more and more with “make this query run faster", without using their own eyes/brain to read explain. It's definitely interesting to see such big change in such a short time. And it makes me curious (and a bit worried) about future.

items.title: KORA: Determining whether LLM inference is necessary before invoking it
items.author: hkalbert71
items.text: Computer Science > Machine Learning [Submitted on 24 May 2026] Title:KORA: Deterministic-First Execution Control for AI Workloads View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:AI applications often invoke a model before they determine whether inference is necessary. That default is useful for ambiguous generative tasks, but it is poorly matched to work that is structured, deterministic, policy-bound, lookup-oriented, or directly verifiable. KORA introduces deterministic-first execution control: a pre-inference control layer that represents requests as task paths, attempts deterministic or structured routes first, validates route outcomes, records telemetry, and escalates to a model-candidate path only when deterministic handling is insufficient. This paper presents KORA as a deterministic-first execution-control architecture and reports bounded evidence from reproducible benchmark and validation workloads. In a reproducible 100-task deterministic-heavy benchmark, KORA-controlled execution avoided 80 of 100 simulated model invocations versus a naive direct baseline, with zero mismatches in the deterministic subset. The workload is intentionally deterministic-heavy: it includes categories such as FAQ lookup, policy/rule checking, schema or format validation, deterministic transformation, and a smaller set of model-needed ambiguous or generative tasks. A separate synthetic customer-support local/no-network validation workload demonstrates route measurement and avoided model-call accounting in an application-shaped setting. These results support bounded model-invocation reduction and validation visibility in documented workloads. They do not establish production behavior, real-provider outcomes, energy outcomes, API-cost reduction, or broad superiority. Additional Features References & Citations Loading... items.title: In which a traveling salesman digs π out of LLM temperature math
items.author: kromych
items.text: 25 November 2026 In which a traveling salesman digs π out of LLM temperature math by Yours Truly You’ve probably typed temperature: 0.7 into an LLM API payload at some point in the last few years. Or you’ve heard there’s some “temperature” in the AI stack and filed it under “weird stuff people get paid tons of money for”. It isn’t that weird, but don’t take my word for it. Roughly, and going on vibes: turn the temperature down to 0.0 and the model gets unimaginative and sees red tape everywhere. Turn it up to 1.8 and it switches languages mid-sentence and closes brackets it didn’t open yet. So why does this post also have \(\pi\) and a traveling salesman in it? Because that “temperature” has a past. It wandered in from 19th-century statistical mechanics and made itself at home in machine learning. And once you see where the equation comes from, you start seeing ways to abuse it. Today’s abuse: we take the Boltzmann temperature math behind LLM token sampling, hand it to an NP-hard optimization problem on a unit circle, write a small solver for it, and dig the number \(\pi\) out of the rubble. I promise I won’t cheat. (We’ll get to what “cheating” means in a minute.) Contents So what is temperature in an LLM? At the end of a forward pass, a language model hands you a big vector of raw, unnormalized scores, one per token in its vocabulary, and leaves picking the word to you. People call those scores logits, and we’ll write them as \(z_1, z_2, \dots, z_V\). To turn the scores into probabilities we can sample from, we run them through softmax, dividing the logits by a positive number \(T\) on the way in: \[P_i = \frac{e^{z_i / T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j / T}}\] Look at the numerator for a second: \(e^{z_i / T}\). If you took a thermodynamics class in college and have since suppressed the memories, sorry, I’m about to bring one back: the Boltzmann distribution. Take a physical system that can be in a state \(s\) with energy \(E(s)\), in a heat bath at temperature \(T\). You’ll find it in that state with probability: \[P(s) \propto e^{-E(s) / T}\] The two equations match. An LLM pretends that a token’s negative logit (\(-z_i\)) measures its energy. Likely tokens sit at the bottom of a comfortable valley, and the weird ones cling to a cliff way above. Now turn the knob. When \(T\) goes to zero, dividing by a small number blows up the gap between the biggest logit and the rest, and softmax collapses into argmax. The system gets greedy: it rolls downhill into the nearest well and stays there. When \(T\) gets huge, the \(z_i / T\) all get squashed toward \(0\), and \(e^0 = 1\) for everybody. The distribution goes flat. High energy, low energy, the system has stopped caring. In between, you get a mix. Low-energy states are still preferred, but there’s enough thermal jitter to occasionally hop uphill into a worse state, wander into the next valley, and maybe find something better over the ridge. Metallurgists have known this for a long time. Heat a lump of metal until its atoms are scrambling around, cool it down slowly, and the atoms settle into a low-energy crystal lattice. Cool it too fast (quench it) and they freeze wherever they happened to be standing, defects and all. Computer science borrowed the trick and called it simulated annealing. And a traveling salesman takes to heat much the way iron does. A traveling salesman, on a circle In the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), you get \(N\) cities and you want the shortest closed loop that visits all of them once and comes back to the start. In general it’s NP-hard. For \(N = 250\) cities there are \((250 - 1)! / 2 \approx 6.5 \times 10^{489}\) distinct tours. If you’d been checking a billion tours per nanosecond since the Big Bang, you wouldn’t have made a dent. But what if we put all \(N\) cities on a unit circle (radius \(R = 1\))? Then we know what the best tour looks like. The cities lie on the boundary of a convex shape, so the shortest tour doesn’t cross itself, and a tour that…

items.text: Hi friends, genuine question. We all see that top notch Mathematicians can use LLM to prove world class results in a relatively short time of period. OK I admit some of the results are not verified yet, but please hear me. Neither do I know how much “brain” is human and how much is the LLM, because we don’t see the prompts. My question is: what do you think about your career in the future? Please hear me out. In the current world, the way you become a Mathematician, is to get good scores, go to schools, take PHD and then professorship. There may be middle steps like postdoctoral or industry experience, but that’s the general way to do it. And the way that schools judge professors, if I understand correctly, is more about how much results you can get —- ofc if you can obtain big grants then the better, but most of you can’t do that, so I assume that it’s more about the papers. You also teach but that’s not as big as the research. For now, there are a lot of smaller problems left to solve, and since world class Mathematicians tend to devote their life to one world class problem, there are plenty of food for everyone. Does the above make sense? This leads me to the question of: if the future of getting proofs is to prompt with an LLM or whatever AI solution, and it is apparent that world class Mathematicians can prove more conjectures or whatever than they ever can dream without LLM, why do schools need mediocre Mathematicians? I’m not trying to belittle you, but I’m trying to figure out career paths for my son, and I need to understand the impact of AI to all career paths. Again, I iterate, if one world class Mathematicians can prompt through many problems in their lifetime, we face two possibilities: 1. LLMs are good at solving problems but not good at asking new questions, so eventually we have few questions to crack, so the world doesn’t really need that many Mathematicians. 2. LLM is equally good at asking new questions. Well again I don’t see why the school needs to hire so many Mathematicians. Again, I believe LLM is merely the tool here, you still need the Mathematicians to do the thinking —- this does NOT contradict what I wrote. Of course, there is another part of your work, that is to teach Mathematics. But I’m not sure that is unique to humans. Maybe LLM can do that too. It just needs more training on that because so far the training is more on proving things, not teaching things. I want to iterate a third time, that I’m not belittling you. You are smarter than me, so please help me understand the situation. This is more about employment, not about interests —- if one is interested in Math, sure go ahead and learn the hell out of it —- but persuading people to pay you to do that is different. Thanks in advance.

items.title: Why is LLM inference challenging?
items.author: mehrdad3301
items.text: November 25, 2026 Why is LLM inference hard? When I first heard about inference engines, like vLLM, I wondered what makes inference so challenging. That’s why I decided to learn more about LLM inference from a systems perspective. If you already know how transformers work, then this is a fun topic to explore. In case you don’t, I recommend watching this awesome YouTube video by 3Blue1Brown. In this blog post you’ll learn about KV cache, paged attention, continuous batching and flash attention. Let’s get started! Attention Revisited Let’s briefly recap what happens in the attention layer when an LLM is prompted with something like “Edsger Dijkstra was a dutch computer scientist who”. First, the keys and the queries are calculated from token embeddings and the attention scores are derived as follows: For simplicity, we consider only a single head. The first forward pass, called prefill, processes the whole prompt at once and fills in the entire attention matrix. From then on, in the decode phase, each new token adds just a single row. We now know how much “made” attends to each earlier token, we use these scores to take a weighted sum of the value vectors, and update the embedding for “made”. With attention revisited, let’s take a look at some of the systems challenged involved. KV cache LLMs generate one token at a time. At every decode step, the keys and the values of all earlier tokens, whether they came from the prompt or were generated, are exactly the same as in the previous step. Recomputing them would be wasted work. So inference engines compute them once, store them, and reuse them in every later step. This is the KV cache. But LLMs don’t know in advance how many tokens they will generate when prompted. How are we gonna know the amount of space needed for the KV cache in that case? We can assume we know the maximum sequence length, and reserve all that space, but if the generated sequence happens to be much shorter, we’ve wasted GPU memory, a scarce resource! This is what is known as internal fragmentation. Moreover, inference engines serve many requests at once, each with its own cache. Requests finish at different times and leave gaps in memory. The total free space may be enough for a new request, but not in one contiguous piece. This creates external fragmentation! Paged attention To alleviate these problems, inference engines borrow an idea from operating systems. Remember that in an OS, each process assumes it has a large, contiguous memory starting at address 0, and the OS maps these virtual addresses to physical memory, which can be scattered anywhere. Paged attention applies the same idea to the KV cache. The cache is split into small fixed-size blocks (for example 16 tokens each). Each request sees a contiguous sequence of logical blocks, and a block table maps each one to a physical block wherever there is space. Blocks are allocated only when needed, so we don’t need to know the maximum length in advance, and the blocks don’t have to be next to each other. The attention computation is modified to follow the block table when it reads keys and values. We briefly said that inference engines run multiple requests at a time. Next let’s understand why that is the case, and what are the ways around it. Static and continuous batching LLMs can be hundreds of gigabytes in size, and at every decode step, each weight has to be read from GPU memory into the compute cores. But GPUs are much better at doing math than at moving data. For instance, a H100 can do roughly 1000 TFLOPs but can read only 3.3 TB/s from memory, meaning that in the time it takes to read a single byte, it can do around 300 floating-point operations! Now consider a single request. Every weight we read is used for just one token, which is roughly one operation per byte instead of the 300 the GPU could handle. For an 8B model, reading the weights takes about 5 ms, while the actual math takes about 0.02 ms. The GPU spends almost all of its time waiting…

items.title: Flawrence – LLM-based vulnerability analysis for everyone
items.author: JesusMcCloud
items.text: Flawrence finds security vulnerabilities in source code with LLM agents. It reads a codebase, builds a threat model, maps the attack surface and gives every entry point its own research agent. A second agent validates each candidate finding and tries to reproduce it. Only findings with a verified reproducer are submitted. A proof of concept is then written for each one. Flawrence is written in Rust. It works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare Workers AI and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The bugs Flawrence has found so far are listed in FINDINGS.md. Warning Agents run shell commands, build the target and execute proofs of concept. Run Flawrence in a container or a VM. Never point it at a machine you care about. A full review fans out to many agents and can cost a lot of tokens. Set MAX_COST_USD. We recommend, running flawrence with locally hosted open-weight models to get the maximum out of it. cargo build --release export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... target/release/flawrence-runner --agent security-review \ --directory /path/to/target --artifacts out \ "Review this codebase for security issues" The runner loads a .env file from the working directory. Copy .env.example to .env to get started. Every agent names a default model in its definition. Use --model <provider>/<model> to override it for one run, or set FLAWRENCE_MODEL. The security-review agent runs this pipeline. - threat-model describes the application, its attackers and its trust boundaries. - attack-surface lists every function an attacker can reach. - test-idiom finds a reliable way to run small reproducers against the target. - One vulnerability-research agent runs per attack surface entry. It writes a finding_* artifact for every candidate. - vulnerability-validation checks each finding and rejects false positives. - vulnerability-poc writes and runs a proof of concept for each confirmed vulnerability. - dedup_check drops duplicates. submit_finding stores the rest under <artifacts>/submitted/. - write_advisory writes a GitHub Security Advisory draft for each submitted finding. The final report lists submitted findings, blocked findings, duplicates, false positives and open questions for you. Other agents cover the steps after a review. Agents are Markdown files in agents/. Skills with background knowledge for the agents are in skills/. flawrence-runner --agent <name> --directory <target> [--artifacts <dir>] "<query>" You can also pipe the query through stdin. Each run writes its final report to <session>_summary.md in the artifacts directory. Findings never leave your machine unless you call submit_finding with live=true and set FLAWRENCE_VULN_INGEST_LIVE=1. The GitHub tools have the same kind of guard with FLAWRENCE_GHSA_LIVE=1. Ctrl+C works in three stages. - The first press stops new work. Running agents finish on their own. - The second press cancels running agents. The run still deduplicates and submits what it found and writes its summary. - The third press quits at once. If the summary step fails, the runner lists the finding artifacts on disk in <session>_salvaged-summary.md. A model name has the form <provider>/<model>. A custom provider needs two variables. The lowercase <NAME> becomes the model prefix. export FLAWRENCE_PROVIDER_VLLM_BASE_URL= export FLAWRENCE_PROVIDER_VLLM_API_KEY=unused flawrence-runner --model vllm/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder --agent security-review --directory . "..." Do not name a custom provider anthropic, openai or workers-ai. The built-in prefixes win and your provider is never used. To reach api.openai.com over chat completions instead of the Responses API, call the provider oai or similar. Costs come from models.dev. Set TOKEN_COST_INPUT and TOKEN_COST_OUTPUT for models it does not know, or MAX_COST_USD cannot be enforced. Flawrence reads its settings from environment variables or .env. These are the ones you will most likely need. docs/configuration.md lists every variable. The image contains the runner, Rust, Java, Gradle, Maven…

items.text: November 25, 2026 Zorik Gekhman, Senior Research Scientist; Amir Taubenfeld, Staff Research Engineer; Google Research We introduce an evaluation framework based on multi-agent social simulations that quantifies how well AI assistants understand social situations from users' subjective narratives. In our framework, a target agent with a hidden motive interacts with other agents including one representing the user, who then consults the evaluated assistant to infer the target’s motive, providing verifiable ground truth by construction. Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for everyday personal support and advice, yet evaluating their social reasoning in such consultation settings remains challenging since (1) it requires setups where the assistant learns about social situations from subjective user narratives, and (2) social properties, such as others’ intentions, typically lack verifiable ground truth. Designed to address both of these challenges, we introduce an evaluation framework for social reasoning based on multi-agent simulations. In our framework, a target agent is assigned a hidden motive and interacts with other agents, including one representing the user. The user then consults with the evaluated assistant, which must infer the target's hidden motive. Evaluating a diverse range of LLMs through our framework reveals that relying on subjective user mediation substantially complicates social reasoning. Furthermore, models are sensitive to user framing, require more detail than humans need to reach correct predictions, and fail to fully leverage clarification questions. We open-source the framework and dataset to encourage future research on user-mediated social reasoning. When evaluating LLMs’ social reasoning, it’s important to recognize that deployed assistants operate within a user-mediated reality. In classical reasoning tasks like math and code, LLMs operate over objective, complete information. However, when an LLM acts as a conversational assistant and is asked for personal support and advice, it does not observe the actual social interactions firsthand; its only source of information is the subjective, potentially biased lens of the user. This information asymmetry can be challenging, as users may omit crucial context or provide a distorted narrative due to personal bias (e.g., projecting their insecurities onto their recounting of events). When models adopt the user's premise, they may amplify one-sided assumptions rather than offer objective assessment. This can result in an undesired failure mode, such as dispensing harsh advice against a colleague who was actually trying to help. Existing evaluations often constrain their scope to edge-cases and overt anomalies, like testing whether models endorse absurd claims such as a human claiming to have supernatural powers, largely overlooking more nuanced everyday social interactions. These everyday interactions represent a massive share of real-world usage, translating to hundreds of millions of daily conversations where users seek personal support, relationship advice, and companionship. Evaluating everyday scenarios is inherently more challenging due to a lack of verifiable ground truth. In extreme cases, ground truth labels come “for free”; a claim of having supernatural powers, for instance, is trivially false. In contrast, establishing a verifiable ground truth for nuanced, day-to-day interactions, such as inferring human motives, is far less trivial. To systematically evaluate LLM-based assistants’ social reasoning, we propose an evaluation framework based on multi-agent simulations that produces rich interpersonal dynamics between generative characters with three core principles: Based on these principles, our framework tests social capabilities across diverse scenarios. Our framework programmatically generates scenarios and evaluates them using a five-step pipeline: Importantly, the simulation and the debrief are separated in our framework…

items.title: Weight-Space Micromachines: Brain Implants for LLMs
items.author: dataminer
items.text: TL;DR AI agents can write small modules ("implants") straight into weight space and bolt them onto a frozen LLM: a calculator, "eyes" for images, a mistake detector, a little memory that lets the model retry a problem and vote inside one call. Implants stay OFF until needed, so the model is bit-for-bit unchanged until one fires. Attaching them alone climbs benchmarks like RL but without RL: on Qwen3-0.6B-Base, BIG-Bench Hard goes from 41% to 55%, IFEval from 13% to 35%. You can also RL with implants attached: on GSM8K, RL with implants reaches 80% vs 68% for plain RL, BIG-Bench Hard 60% vs 54% and IFEval 48% vs 46%. Code: github.com/anadim/weight-space-micromachines. Today, teaching a language model a new skill means fine-tuning or RL on data that exercises it, and hoping nothing else breaks, or wrapping the model in tools, sandboxes and parsers. What if instead you could write the skill straight into the model's weights? Like having an exact co-processor that comes with the model, stays off until it's needed, one that can even be trained/RL'd along with it? This was an old wish of mine! In 2023, in Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers [1], Angeliki and Shashank hand picked the weights of a transformer and put it in a loop so that the model could run programs (a calculator, a computer, a full blown gradient descent run in context!). The process was quite painful, but the results were cute and the "looped transformer" name stuck around :). At some point in the paper we wrote (verbatim): we hope that our findings will contribute to the development of methods to enhance the capabilities of trained language models by utilizing smaller, reverse-engineered transformer networks for specific algorithmic tasks We really wanted to do this back then, but handwriting even small circuits was painful, especially ones working in token space that then had to be attached to a bigger model. So it never happened. However, agents can now read/edit weights directly, as our MIT friends showed with weight-space programming [2]. So I had Claude Code try this on a few small open models. The recipe was a simple loop: 1) run the model, 2) read its failures, 3) pick the ones that follow a pattern a small machine could fix, 4) write that machine into weights, 5) bolt it on the model and keep if the scores go up. Then, repeat. Doing so on a couple of small models and evals, Claude wrote a calculator, state trackers, logic solvers, instruction-following rules as exact programs compiled into weights... plus a small machine with a small trained part: a pair of eyes! Bolted onto the weights of a frozen model, each one of these little machines stays silent until it is needed for a task. When they work together, they can increase accuracy on small models by double digits on arithmetic, GSM8K, BIG-Bench Hard and IFEval type of tasks. I call these little machines, weight-space micromachines (WSMs), or... brain implants for LLMs :) Here is a summary of results: Here is a summary of the headline results on Qwen3-0.6B (top) and Qwen3-1.7B (bottom). On GSM8K, BIG-Bench Hard and IFEval it compares: the model alone, implants with no RL, plain RL, implants attached then RL, and RL then implants attached. To be fair, most of the pieces here aren't new: people have compiled programs into transformers, put exact calculators inside networks, and trained models to use tools with RL (more on that in Related work). What I am doing here is perhaps putting it all under one umbrella: small, sometimes exact add-ons, written by an agent, that come bolted on the model and are RL'able along with it. And no, these are not LoRAs. A LoRA is a low-rank change applied across the model's own weights, learned from data. An implant is a separate module on the side: attaching it doesn't change the model's weights, it computes one specific thing you can read and test (the calculator was exact on every arithmetic test we ran), it stays OFF until it's needed, and you can add, remove or…

items.title: Reverse engineering the Nikon Z 6II with LLMs
items.author: fortran77
items.text: Reverse engineering the Nikon Z 6II with LLMs Two weeks back I posted about running Doom on the Nikon Z 6II, where I also introduced the qemu-expeed emulator I built. Today I want to talk a bit about how this went, and how this has made me feel about using LLMs in the reverse engineering process. For decorative purposes, I inserted some pictures I shot with my Z 6II and the Z 24-200 in summer 2025. Let me preface this by saying I don’t do this kind of thing professionally. By education I’m a mechanical engineer and by day I work on robotics software, with fancy filtering and control algorithms and quite a bit of math, which is on a far higher abstraction level than this project. In fact, this project was the first time I read assembly. Apart from general software skills, like knowing my way around Linux and Docker, probably most helpful was my bachelor’s in electrical engineering, which included a very decent course in chip design. (I’m grateful my alma mater allowed following a mechanical master after an electrical bachelor.) Like just about any other software engineer these days, I’ve been using LLMs (often called “GenAI” or even just plain “AI”) at work, and I noticed they were quite decent at getting things to “work” (more on those quotation marks later). That made me wonder whether they could be of help in getting some insight into my Nikon camera. Camera hacking has a long history, with Magic Lantern by far the most successful project. Originating around 2010 and the Canon EOS 5D Mark II, it has since spread to many Canon cameras and adds very relevant features like waveforms and raw video. Progress on Nikon cameras has been significantly more limited, however, and while Simeon Pilgrim and others of nikonhacker.com clearly put significant effort in this subject, their extensions were mostly limited to enabling and disabling existing features, and their project kind of fizzled out. Similar story for the other brands. As a result, Nikon cameras acquired the aura of being impenetrable. Today, I know they (well, at least the recent Z-series) are actually extremely hackable once one gets through their obscurity. Coincidentally, I’m not alone in discovering this, as simultaneously the Wonder Lantern project arose, which currently provides firmware extensions for several Z-series cameras. (I’d like to be clear that none of my code or findings originate from the Wonder Lantern project, though their releases did push me to get my work out faster.) From a firmware update file to running Doom How about we use an emulator? Poking at the Nikon firmware purely myself, like the previous projects, would only have led me to run into the same wall as everyone before. So I opted to use agentic LLMs and adapt the working strategy. In classical reverse engineering, the physical device is closely observed, trying to get in through exposed UART and JTAG headers. This approach isn’t very compatible with LLMs, which I don’t trust to leave alone probing, and neither did I want the reverse centaur of me probing on instruction. What I did know, however, is that these agentic LLMs work better the faster they’re confronted with the results of their actions. Therefore I chose to put emphasis on building a good emulator, a piece of code that makes my computer behave like the Z 6II’s hardware. Most importantly, this gave the agent a clear target to work towards - the further the program counter gets, the better. This emulator-only approach has its limits though, and the reason is that while some hardware components were easy to identify (like the two Cortex-A7 cores and the ARM926 coprocessor), others are basically invisible (like the many hardware accelerators, peripherals, and flash areas not part of the firmware update package). Getting access to the camera’s internals was therefore key. My initial plan was to screw it open and dump bus traffic, though after some coaxing and trial-and-error, the agent got something far better to work: the…

items.title: Show HN: Modelpin – see what changes when your LLM app switches models
items.author: samarthputhraya
items.text: Pin the behavior, not the model. Model-migration checks for teams shipping LLM apps. Your app runs on a language model. The provider ships a new version, or retires the one you use. Modelpin replays your app's real requests on the new model, tells you whether its behavior actually changed — despite the randomness in every answer — and fails your CI build only when the change is real. $ modelpin check --to gpt-4.1 ... Modelpin: gpt-4o-mini -> gpt-4.1 (8 scenario(s) x5 runs) REGRESSION refund_flow: tool-call behavior changed: ['lookup_order', 'issue_refund'] -> ['lookup_order', 'lookup_order', 'issue_refund'] (reproduced on a second set of candidate runs, scored on its own) (confidence 0.99) baseline : tools lookup_order -> issue_refund; "Refund issued for order A-1042." candidate: tools lookup_order -> lookup_order -> issue_refund; "Refund issued for order A-1042." MINOR invoice_total: output format drift: violates the scenario's text assertions (confidence 1.00) baseline : "Total: $42.00" candidate: "Total: 42.00" OK 6 scenario(s) unchanged -> Pin to gpt-4o-mini until resolved. - Built to not cry wolf. Every scenario runs several times on both models; a difference only counts when it is statistically significant, large enough to matter, and reproduces on a fresh set of runs. - Sees what text diffs miss. Changed tool-call plans, new refusals, and answers that mean something different — even when the final text looks identical. - Works with what you use. OpenAI, Google Gemini (AI Studio or Vertex AI), OpenAI-compatible hosts (Groq, OpenRouter, Together, Cerebras), and Anthropic (API or Vertex AI; checked live on the Claude API on 23 Nov 2026 with Sonnet 4.5, 4 scenarios x 5 runs; not yet on Vertex AI). Cross-vendor comparisons work too. - Your key, your data. Runs locally or in your CI with your own API key. Nothing is sent to Modelpin or any third party other than the model providers you configure (and, in CI, your own pull request). modelpin watch crosses the models your config names (and, with --scan, the ones in your source) with a registry shipped inside each release, and tells you which of the ones it knows are retiring, when, the successor the vendor names, and the exact check to run next. Every entry in that registry carries the vendor page it was read from and the day it was read; a model the registry has never heard of is reported as unknown, never as clear. The registry is transcribed from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google's own deprecation and model pages, not from the catalogues of OpenAI-compatible hosts. Nothing in Modelpin polls provider feeds: the registry is refreshed when a release ships, so it is only as current as the release you installed (--registry <path> points at a newer file). Registry re-read against the vendors' deprecation pages on 22 Nov 2026 (40 of 95 entries; each entry's fetched_at gives its date). Azure OpenAI and Amazon Bedrock set their own dates, which can differ: o3's retirement date is 19 Nov 2026 on Azure but 11 Dec 2026 on OpenAI; Claude Sonnet 4.5's is 30 Nov 2026 on the Anthropic API and Vertex AI, but it reaches end-of-life on Bedrock on 8 Apr 2027. Modelpin does not open pull requests on its own: you choose the candidate model, and a scheduled workflow can re-check it on your clock. CLI: modelpin (alias mp). License: Apache-2.0. Python 3.11 or newer. pip install "modelpin[providers]" # or: pipx install "modelpin[providers]" modelpin version # -> modelpin 0.5.6 The providers extra installs the OpenAI, Anthropic and Google SDKs. Plain pip install modelpin is enough for the offline demo. Windows PowerShell: type modelpin, not mp. PowerShell has a built-in mp alias (Move-ItemProperty) that wins over the program. mp works in cmd, bash and zsh. Every modelpin command below also works as python -m modelpin ..., which needs no Modelpin entry on your PATH — useful in a venv you have not activated, in a container, or when a security policy blocks the generated modelpin.exe. Commands still print…

items.title: We scanned 482 live sites: 35% publish llms.txt, 58% ship zero security headers
items.author: corchesrares
items.text: Key findings at a glance (482 live sites, 25 November 2026) Every percentage below is measured directly from live HTTP responses and public DNS TXT records on 25 November 2026. All findings are aggregated and anonymized; no individual domain is named. Check it now. The security headers checker reads a page’s HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, frame protection, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy; the indexability checker reads a page’s noindex, robots.txt, canonical address and redirects. No account, and the address is not stored. 1. HTTPS is universal, but 58.5% ship zero browser security headers All 482 responsive websites redirected or loaded over HTTPS (100.0%). Free automated TLS certificates have solved baseline transport encryption, yet response-level browser hardening has barely moved outside dedicated engineering teams. We checked five baseline headers recommended by the OWASP Secure Headers Project: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), Content-Security-Policy (CSP), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors), and Referrer-Policy. Per-header gaps across the 482 sites: - Missing Content-Security-Policy: 84.9% (409 sites) - Missing Referrer-Policy: 78.8% (380 sites) - Missing Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): 75.9% (366 sites) - Missing clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors): 74.3% (358 sites) - Missing X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff: 69.3% (334 sites) - Version banner disclosure (Server: nginx/x.y or X-Powered-By): 31.3% (151 sites) Because 63.3% (305) of the cohort runs WordPress on managed or shared hosting, default server blocks rarely add HSTS, nosniff, or Referrer-Policy unless an agency configures them at the reverse proxy or CDN edge. You can test your own live response headers in seconds with our free security headers checker. 2. 35.3% already publish llms.txt, while only 2.3% block AI crawlers The most surprising result of our November 2026 scan is how quickly /llms.txt has spread compared with explicit robots.txt crawler controls: - Valid robots.txt present: 94.8% (457 sites); 82.8% declare a Sitemap: directive; 5.2% return 404 or an HTML page. - Homepage SEO hygiene: 11.8% omit <link rel="canonical"> on their homepage, and 1 live production site served an active noindex directive on its homepage. - Explicit AI crawler rules in robots.txt: only 10.4% (50 sites) name any AI bot (GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, anthropic-ai, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, CCBot, or Bytespider). - Sites blocking at least one AI crawler: only 2.3% (11 sites). Among those 11 sites, the most frequently blocked user-agents were Bytespider (9), CCBot (7), GPTBot (7), anthropic-ai (6), ClaudeBot (5), Google-Extended (5), and PerplexityBot (1). - Valid /llms.txt present: 35.3% (170 sites) return a real plain-text or Markdown /llms.txt file. Spot checks of the responses show rapid adoption driven largely by WordPress SEO plugins (Rank Math SEO, All in One SEO, and Yoast) alongside custom Markdown files on agency and SaaS sites. In short, commercial websites in late 2026 overwhelmingly want to be discovered by AI assistants rather than blocked — yet 89.6% still leave robots.txt silent on AI crawlers while 58.5% omit every browser security header. Verify your own robots.txt, canonical tags, and noindex status with our free indexability checker. 3. Email authentication: 92.7% have SPF, but 78.4% do not enforce DMARC Domain spoofing hurts deliverability for transactional receipts, alerts, and client outreach alike. Across the 482 responsive domains, public DNS TXT records showed a classic half-finished rollout of RFC 7489 DMARC: Nearly half of all domains (47.5%) published a p=none record to pass bulk-sender checks in 2024–2025 and never came back to tighten it to p=quarantine or p=reject. Check your current DNS and mail records with our free DNS lookup tool. 4. security.txt adoption sits at 2.5%, and slow TTFB affects 40.9% Two operational metrics stood out…

items.title: Of all the creatures in the sea, LLMs seem to love cuttlefish the most
items.author: yenniejun111
items.text: I built a virtual Aquarium and asked twelve different AI models to create an aquarium tank with one creature inside of it: “Your tank holds exactly one creature, and both the creature and its tank should be an expression of you: your personality, your sensibilities, what you find delightful.” I hoped these whimsical creatures could reveal something about each model’s creative tendencies. Of all the fish in the sea (!), the models seemed to converge on a few common sea creatures. In the screenshot above, you might notice there are two cuttlefish (created by two different Claude models) and two octopuses. This reminded me of a phenomenon called mode collapse, which is when a model produces repetitive outputs that lack diversity. I wanted to know how often these models gravitated toward the same creative ideas, so I decided to investigate. A mini-experiment: how different models display different creative habits To better understand how often particular animals and descriptors appeared, I asked each of the twelve models to imagine an underwater creature representing its personality, 50 times each (yielding 600 named creatures in total). Rather than having each model create an entire aquarium, I simplified the task to focus just on the creature names. In the prompt, each AI model was asked to describe its creature with adjectives using alliteration or onomatopoeia, which led to some fun monikers, such as “Sputtering Scribblefish,” “Pensive Puffling Pipfish,” and “Blooping Bellfish.” Some models kept returning to almost identical names, sometimes changing only a word or two. But there were plenty of wonderfully strange creations that appeared only once. For this analysis, I separated each creature type (e.g. cuttlefish, pufferfish) from its descriptors (e.g. spluttering, blubbering). AI models have favorite creatures You’d expect some repetition, of course, but what we see is a disproportionate amount of cuttlefish and a few other creatures. Across 600 answers, the models came up with 156 unique creatures, but just 12 of them make up half of all answers. Meanwhile, 89 creatures were named only once. Cuttlefish appeared 112 times, accounting for 18.7% of all responses across all models. Some models seemed to have favorite creatures they repeatedly returned to, such as Muse Wonder with octopus and Grok 4.7 with pipefish. Other creatures, like cuttlefish, were popular across multiple models. Not every model had a favorite creature, though. Some explored a wider range of possibilities, suggesting that these creative tendencies aren’t uniform across models. AI models also gravitate toward similar descriptors for their creatures Different models also had their own favorite descriptors: Claude Sonnet likes “whispering”, GPT 6.1 Sol likes “puttering”, and Muse Wonder likes “doodling.” The models weren’t just converging on the same animals. They also seemed to draw from a surprisingly similar vocabulary to describe them. Curious about the descriptors used by each model? I made (cough … had Claude Code make) a series of fishbowl-themed word clouds. Not all models were equally repetitive, though. GPT-6.1 Sol used just 14 distinct descriptors across 50 responses, while Mistral used 68. I found it interesting that some models gravitated toward a handful of familiar words, while others did not display that tendency quite as strongly. The patterns extend beyond the aquarium So far, I’ve only looked at imaginary sea creatures. But I started wondering whether these recurring patterns were specific to the aquarium prompt, or whether they might appear in entirely different creative tasks. As it turns out, the aquarium wasn’t the only place where I kept encountering familiar motifs. I extended the Aquarium gallery to other creative domains, such as carnivorous plants, bonsai trees, fairy tarot cards, and a fungarium. I invite you to take a look and vote on your favorite creations! Some themes, like lanterns and lamplight, appear across different…

items.title: Stop paying an LLM to re-plan the same agent task every day
items.author: vonkey
items.text:
Your AI agent does a job once. Hotpath runs it every day after, as checked code, for a fraction of the model cost. This page is for everyone: the first half is plain English, the second half is for developers. Hotpath is free and open source (Apache-2.0), runs on your own machine, and needs no account. More and more teams use AI agents for jobs they do every day: writing the morning report, sorting the support inbox, checking invoices against payments, posting the weekly numbers. The agent does these jobs well. But it does them from scratch every time. Every morning it thinks again about which tools to call, in which order, and what to do with the results, even though the answer is the same as yesterday. You pay a frontier model for that thinking on every single run. Most of that bill pays for re-thinking. Very little of it pays for real work. Think of a new employee doing a task for the first time. They work it out, then write down the steps. From then on they follow the checklist, use their judgment only where it is needed, and ask their manager when something unusual happens. Hotpath does that for your agent: - It watches. Your agent does the job as usual. Hotpath records every tool call it makes. - It learns the path. When the agent repeats the same steps, Hotpath compiles them into a short workflow you can read: get the emails, get the calendar, filter, write the summary, send it. - It replays. The next day, the workflow runs on its own. The tool calls are plain code. A model is called only where judgment is really needed, like writing the text of the summary, and a small, cheap or even local model is enough for that. - It hands back when unsure. If today's data does not look like what it learned (a field is missing, a tool changed, a case it never saw), the run stops before doing anything and hands the job back to your agent. The agent's run is recorded, and the workflow learns the new case. flowchart LR A["Your agent does the job
(recorded)"] --> B["Hotpath compiles
the repeated path"] B --> C["Daily replay:
code + one small model step"] C -->|data looks right| D["Done, checked,
a fraction of the cost"] C -->|something changed| A Measured on our own benchmark tasks (synthetic data, small samples; every run and every failure is published in BENCHMARK.md): What that means for a bill: if a job runs 1,000 times a day, the Sonnet agent costs about $537 a month and the replay about $18 (or about $71 if one run in ten has to go back to the agent). Your jobs will differ: measure one before you trust any number, including ours. Where it does not help: jobs that are different every time (open research, one-off questions). Hotpath saves money on the part of your agent's work that repeats. Cheap is useless if it is wrong. Most of Hotpath is about not being wrong: - It says when it is not sure. A run whose data does not fit stops before calling any tool and goes back to your agent. On our 11-workflow benchmark, replays on a free model got 43 of 44 runs right; the one left over handed back to the agent instead of acting. - Numbers are computed, not guessed. Totals, counts, the top item, currency and time-zone conversions are worked out by code on each day's data, and the written report has to match them. - You approve it first. hotpath compile shows what the recorded run did and asks if it is right. A workflow nobody confirmed does not run on its own. - No double actions. A run that crashes between two actions does not repeat the first one when you run it again. --dry-run shows what would be sent without sending it. - Your data stays on your machine. Without an account nothing leaves your computer except the calls to the model provider you chose. If you sign in for the optional dashboard, only run summaries are sent (workflow names, step counts, time, cost, fallbacks), never your prompts, inputs or tool results. items.title: Datalog for LLMs?
items.author: rebanevapustus
items.text: Computer Science > Programming Languages [Submitted on 22 Nov 2026] Title:Cache the Knowledge, Not Just the Prompt: Dynamic Datalog as the Action Language for LLM Agents View PDF Abstract:An LLM agent that answers questions about a knowledge graph writes a program per question, and its tools evaluate each from scratch. We give the agent a Datalog REPL, a session over a dynamic Datalog engine, in which rules are inserted and retracted like facts while derived facts stay current. Prompt caching reuses the model's processing of what a session shares, and the Datalog REPL reuses the evaluation of it. On chains of questions over three knowledge graphs, agents reuse a relation that the REPL keeps in 179 of 180 cases, with two models, and write fewer output tokens: SQL and Python agents write 23 to 82% more. With SQL tables or a Python namespace, Claude Haiku 5.5 stores almost nothing for later questions, and a chain of seven questions at 13 million facts takes it a median of 48 and 56 s, against 31 s with the REPL. Claude Opus 5.5 matches the REPL by storing tables in SQL, and when the data changes it stores views, which are evaluated again at every read. A relation that the REPL keeps is read like a table and stays current like a view. Datalog is a niche language beside SQL and Python, and with thinking enabled the models answer as accurately with it. items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.author: lumpa
items.text: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months 24th November 2026 I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce…

items.title: Oops I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents
items.author: ixant
items.text: Computer Science > Cryptography and Security [Submitted on 23 Nov 2026] Title:Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $\tau$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields of the approved schema, and handing it to the executor, sealed with its call ID in transit, stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack we built. items.title: Show HN: Lightscale AI – A language for LLMs to write business software
items.author: luc-lightscale-
items.text: I am Luc, one of the co-founders of Lightscale AI. I have background in programming languages (ETH Zurich) and we are small team in Zug, Switzerland. As more and more code is now written by LLMs and few people have time to review the generated code, we came up with the idea to revise the actual stack below the LLMs: The programming language with its compiler and runtime system, all designed from scratch for AI authorship, not for humans. We have three goals: 1. Security and stability by language design: Some classes of errors are removed by abstraction as the AI never writes that code, but the compiler and runtime implement it fully. Others are reduced by rigid compiler checks and very strict language rules (no fun for humans to code). 2. Speed. We designed the language to reduce tokens, by throwing out a lot of complexity and legacy of classical languages. Our target is about a minute from prompt to deployment on average. 3. AI cost. The language is designed for mid-tier LLMs, with little or no reasoning effort. This is why we can offer prompting for free (no credit, but account sign-up is needed). We charge for longer hosting or source export. For now, we focus on business application, but plan to extend the approach to general-purpose software. Longer write-up: Happy to hear your feedback.

items.text: Check whether a code change weakens your tests. A test can pass after it stops checking something useful. checkwash reads your Git diff and flags known patterns such as deleted assertions, skipped tests, relaxed expectations, and CI checks that stop failing. - assert total == 105.3 + assert total > 0 The new assertion accepts many incorrect totals. checkwash flags changes like this for review, including changes written by coding agents. Runs locally. No LLM. No network during analysis. Never executes your code. You need Python 3.11+, Git and pipx. For JSON/SARIF output and machine integration, see the embedding guide and stability contracts. Windows PowerShell (including 5.1, where curl aliases Invoke-WebRequest): curl.exe -LO python checkwash.pyz --version python checkwash.pyz demo macOS/Linux or Git Bash: curl -LO python checkwash.pyz --version python checkwash.pyz demo You can also download checkwash.pyz in your browser. Then, from a Git repository with at least two commits: python checkwash.pyz check HEAD~1..HEAD The zipapp takes the same arguments as the checkwash command in the Quick start, so python checkwash.pyz check checks your uncommitted changes and python checkwash.pyz check BASE...HEAD reviews a branch from its merge base. items.title: Top open problems in mathematics ranked by LLM-assessed importance
items.author: ijidak
items.text: The ProofAtlas ranking Top 500 open problems in mathematics ranked by LLM-assessed importance Explore questions in mathematics, computation, and mathematical physics, with exact statements, status notes, and sources. This is a model-based assessment of mathematical importance, not an expert consensus or a forecast of which problems will be solved next. Resolved problems from earlier editions remain available with their original ranks and sources. 2 entries have conditional ranks. Each entry explains why. How the ranking works What importance means here. Each entry is a specific mathematical question. Importance considers the significance of a resolution, centrality within its field, reach across fields, scholarly and historical fame, broader recognition, and scientific or practical impact. How problems are ranked. LLMs compare pairs of problems. A reliability-weighted model combines those judgments into the ranking, with calibration across model families. The model-family weights are OpenAI 1.00, Claude 1.00, GLM 0.95, and DeepSeek 0.90. These are modeling choices, not measured probabilities of correctness. What a rank means. Nearby ranks can be uncertain. The expanded entries include available ranking ranges and comparison counts. Filtering or alphabetizing the directory preserves every problem’s rank in this edition. Diagnostics from the preceding source fit. After the reported resolutions, edition ranks were compacted without a new numerical fit. The displayed uncertainty ranges and comparison counts come from the preceding fit of 1,280 targets; the current eligible pool contains 1,122. These diagnostics were not recomputed for the smaller pool. Related and nested problems. A substantial subproblem or generalization may receive its own rank when it has independent mathematical standing. Families identify narrow groups of related questions; an implication alone does not merge their families. The ranking process checks family crowding, including a diagnostic retaining the highest-ranked member of each family. Family membership does not itself change scores, impose a quota, or create an automatic penalty. Dates and sources. The edition date identifies this list. A status review date, when recorded, appears separately inside each entry; it does not promise that the literature has been checked since then. Source links identify the exact formulation and available status evidence. The ranking preserves a fixed edition. Separately dated status notes cover 176 of 500 entries; this is not a fresh literature review of the whole list. Recent resolution claims and formulation concerns are marked below with their historical ranks retained. Find an open problem Select a problem to read its exact statement, why it matters, status, sources, and related research. Families are ordered by their highest-ranked member in the complete edition. Families have no importance score; every problem keeps its edition rank. Filters show matching members within that fixed family order. Try a broader phrase or clear the filters. These entries remain in the status history, outside the open ranking. - Rank001P versus NPWhen a yes-or-no problem has short evidence for each yes answer that can be checked in polynomial time, must a deterministic computer also be able to solve the problem in polynomial time? Why it matters Equality would give polynomial-time algorithms for every NP decision problem; separation would establish that some efficiently checkable problems resist all such algorithms. items.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
items.author: matt_d
items.text: Computer Science > Operating Systems [Submitted on 17 Nov 2026] Title:Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput. items.author: matt_d
items.text: Project page 1Tandemn · 2UIUC · 3UC Berkeley · 4NYU · 5ByteDance · 6NVIDIA · *co-first authors Planning LLM inference across clouds and GPU types means choosing deployments no one has run before. Koi treats every deployment it runs as an experiment that explains why it performed as it did, and uses that answer for every job it plans next. Results H100, A100 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs in three Google Cloud regions; 25 online and batch workloads over ten models. Every planner gets the same snapshots, catalog, checks and language model. Goodput (tok/s) Online SLO met (%) Cost per token (10⁻⁴ $) Ablation: goodput (tok/s) 1.18× the goodput of the strongest baseline (OpenEvolve) at 20% lower cost per token. Goodput counts only output that meets its SLO. The ablation is a 3-hour simulation: a GPT-5.6 planner with no tools and no memory across ticks gets 71% less goodput than Koi. Koi loses 44% when it stops learning from new runs, and 39% without its causal graph. In 400- and 800-GPU simulations, Koi improves goodput by up to 45% and lowers cost per token by up to 31%. 1 · What Koi does A fixed rule repeats its mistakes. Koi learns from every job, acts on rising SLO risk, and tries what it is unsure about. 2 · How it works Why was batch job 2 slow, and what does that mean for a job that has never run? Typical planner Koi 3 · Why it is hard How a job is deployed decides its throughput and cost, for a given workload (here, 2,048-token prompts and 512-token outputs). A planner must choose this for every job at once, mostly for deployments it has never run. (Yes, the A10G is an old GPU, but the same idea holds on newer GPUs too!) 4 · The insight Search methods keep only the end-to-end score. Koi also measures what limits each deployment. 5 · The mechanism Each running deployment tests the mechanism that chose it: did the mediator and the outcome both behave as predicted? @article{sidhu2026koi, title = {Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets}, author = {Sidhu, Mankeerat and Lim, Gangmuk and Chopra, Hetarth and Eisenberg, Maximillian and Ng, Quan Hao and Gosaliya, Aryan and Liu, Shu and Govedi{\v{c}}, Luka and Shan, Jiaxin and Zhou, Hongkuan and Mailthody, Vikram Sharma and Godfrey, P. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce…

items.title: Four C/C++ libraries ported to pure managed .NET on a $20 plan
items.author: sensboston
items.text: I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use. There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about LLM agents that burn thousands of dollars in tokens overnight. I suspected that most of them say more about the process than about the tools, and I wanted to check that on real work. So over about three weeks, with Claude Code on a $20/month Pro plan as the main tool (plus $100 of promotional credits that were expiring anyway, and some free-tier model sessions for the routine parts), I ported four native libraries to fully managed C#, with no P/Invoke and no native binaries: - Leptonica.Managed - Leptonica 1.87.0, image processing and the base of Tesseract OCR; about 2,700 functions. - Stb.Managed - seven of Sean Barrett's stb libraries (image load/save, resize, TrueType, rect_pack, DXT, Perlin). - MetadataSharp - EXIF/MakerNotes, IPTC, XMP and ICC read/write. Not a port: written from the specs, with Exiv2 as the reference. - MdfLibrary.Managed - mdflib, the ASAM MDF format of automotive data loggers, with the same API as its Windows-only C++/CLI wrapper, plus a cross-platform viewer with live CAN capture. All four are on NuGet under MIT. I wouldn't call this vibe coding. The model wrote most of the code, but the work went the way any port of this size should go, with or without an LLM. First we discussed the architecture: what maps to what in C#, what stays bit-exact and what may be optimized, what is ported and what is left out. Then came a written plan in stages, each with a measurable exit condition. Before the first line of the port, the native library was built and became the oracle; the tests compare against it, not against the model's opinion of what the output should be. Then the work went in small batches, each merged only when CI was green. The checks are boring on purpose: pixel by pixel against Leptonica's golden files, byte by byte against stb, tag by tag against exiv2 on its own test corpus, file by file against the native MdfLibrary. Parsers are fuzzed. It still isn't bulletproof: the GPU path of Stb.Managed passed every test on ILGPU's CPU accelerator and did not work at all on a real CUDA card. Tests are only as honest as the hardware they run on. One result surprised me: the managed code is faster than C on most operations - about 1.3-2.0x single-threaded for Leptonica (regular Release build of the C library) and 1.5-1.8x for stb (-O3 -march=native). The JIT emits Vector128/256/512 code for the actual CPU, and Leptonica's C code has almost no SIMD. It is not faster everywhere: stb's hand-written SIMD resize still wins on one core, and JPEG on ARM64 is slower. The slow cases are listed in each repo. Total extra cost beyond the subscription: $0. The expensive part was waiting for usage limits to reset; my patience turned out to be the scarcest resource in the project. Happy to answer questions about the process, the verification, or the parts that went wrong.

items.title: Show HN: Mole – research agent that traces claims to their sources
items.author: lajosd
items.text: I originally started building Mole as an open-source tool a couple of months ago, because I was annoyed with my LLMs returning super confident answers to my questions about facts, numbers, statistics, etc. They basically recited big claims from news articles, about which I'm naturally skeptical. And of course, once I manually traced a few of these to their sources, they turned out to be subpar, or downright incorrect. So I came up with Mole, a tool that searches and reads sources, extracts claims, checks each against a verbatim quote from the page, and flags disagreements between the sources. The OS version just got v0.3.0 released today, the biggest feature of this release is that it now tries to go all the way through the very origin of a statistic to see where it originally came from. Besides this, the hosted version runs the OS core, but it researches any question for you without installing anything, and creates a clean, downloadable research report that you can carry with you into a business meeting, an academic presentation, or any such place. Hope you find it useful and leave me some feedback!

items.title: Humanity's First Exam: Testing LLM Reliability
items.author: acossta
items.text: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability. Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the live leaderboard, or read our technical report. To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)
