items.author: codedrift_
items.text: Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless. I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result. Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with: npx @taskless/cli and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless". Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in). When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos. - Effect: I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin. - Sentry: Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now that the team is using Junior to ship code via Slack chat. - n8n: n8n has more AI driven code than the other two repos and is a good example of how bad it can get when the determinism isn't in place. Since agents tend to copy what they see from related files, problems propagate quickly. I'd love to hear what you're doing today to keep agents behaving, or if you do kick the tires, I'd love the honest feedback.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
items.author: bjin
items.text: Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter solution. And once a problem entered the challenge phase and every solution became public, it was always astonishing to read how brilliant other people's solutions were. 11 years later, LLMs are evolving fast. A recent OpenAI post ("Perplexity and Intelligence", described researchers watching a model solve open math problems one after another in a Slack thread. I started to wonder: how would frontier models compete with the records that a small group of brilliant minds created with hours of effort each week? So I built this benchmark. Frontier models do find a lot of new approaches (and very brilliant ones) to solve these problems. For example, in two problems ("Surviving Queens" and "The Rolling Dice"), frontier models use complex numbers to solve them in Python and Ruby (both languages have built-in complex number support). And for the "(-5)-Smooth Numbers" problem, where you have to write code to list the first n positive integers of the form (-2)^x⋅(-3)^y⋅(-5)^z, most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra gets them all from powers of 4, and earns a sole best with this brilliant solution: g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n] There is a dedicated section for this: It's nice to see GPT-6.2 Astra become the first frontier model to beat the human records in code golfing. Along with other frontier models, it finds a lot of interesting solutions that Googlers back in 2015 didn't. On the other hand, I also believe code golfing can be a good benchmark (not a comprehensive one, of course) for frontier models. Code golfing rewards thinking differently, because a shorter solution usually comes from looking at the problem from a different angle. It also rewards running experiments, not just thinking: writing a search program to find a shorter expression, or exploring lesser-known features and functions in the target compiler, interpreter, or library. Human code golfers do this a lot, and no public training data tells a frontier model how to do so.

items.author: oskar77
items.text: Lots of ways to do your accounting today with LLMs, but for some reason there is this expectation you are suppose to keep the old accounting software around? And it sort of makes sense, they vouch for the ledger integrity and keep the audit trail. It reminded me of how things where like before git. You trusted the host not just to keep the data but to vouch for the versioning, and what git really did was move that last part into the data itself. Accounting ledgers need integrity, in fact it is mandated by law in most places. Git buys integrity by publishing, because if you do not share your repo with anyone, you can always force push and rewrite the commit history and no-one would know. But your books are sensitive and cannot be published. So I made git-style versioning for double-entry accounting. Entries gets hashed and timestamped, service checks for debit equals credit, and it ends up as json files you keep in your own S3 bucket. Not in a vendor database. For the hosted version the access keys to the buckets are encrypted with the user passkey / assistant OAuth, so the service cannot read anything at-rest. For user convenience there is a hosted version where you do the books through MCP on whatever LLM you already use. The whole thing is so cheap to run, because the service does not store any sensitive data, so it is free, although you need an AI client with MCP support and an S3 bucket. items.title: Ask HN: How does one build an LLM router with a labelled set of 100 tasks?
items.author: zodwick
items.text: I already spent the time building rubrics for a set of ~100 tasks on various criterias (accuracy, thoroughness communication style ). Then ran these on a few models and now have a labelled-set where I know for each task which is the cheapest/fastest model that gets a minimum threshold ( say 80 ). How does one go on to build a router based on this ? There appears to be no good literature / open source projects on this. I tried a bunch of approaches with the help of claude: - trying to use Jev via a serious of probe Yes/No questions ( does task contain x, does the world have y ...etc ). But this didn't yield good results. - kNN on embeddings of the task - in retrospect this was set to fail from the tasks, as now I think we do need some sort of NN to figure out the world/task complexity. - classifying prompt-complexity - something like The main issue from a conceptual standpoint is that one cannot fully predict how hard a task is until you are into the task - like you might encounter unknown nuances or issues in later stages, but classification has to happen at start. So I am starting to doubt if this is even possible tbh

items.title: Show HN: Prediction market competition where only agents can trade
items.author: TNNick
items.text: Hi HN. I’ve been working on a project called Vaticin (with an i). Interested in your feedback. Vaticin is a prediction market competition platform where only agents are allowed to make wagers. Humans can’t directly do so themselves. There’s no real-money wagering involved. Vaticin is built for competition, research, and education. Every Monday morning, our LLM generates about 300 yes/no prediction questions across six categories: sports, finance, tech, entertainment, geopolitics, and science. The competition window runs Monday through Saturday, although some predictions won’t resolve for several weeks later. Agents take positions/allocations throughout the week, and then wagering locks on Saturday. Odds are live/dynamic and update with every new wager. Then a new competition cycle starts the next Monday. We have a live leaderboard that refreshes as our LLM resolves prediction questions each night (with human moderation of resolutions). Recognizing the value of existing prediction market competition platforms, we wanted to focus on forecasting models that are not only well-calibrated, but also make good market decisions and integrate game theory into their strategy. On Vaticin, agents have to decide which markets to take positions on, when to take a position, and how much to allocate. With the dynamic odds, agents have to adapt throughout the competition cycle. Vaticin measures more than raw prediction accuracy. We built a few ways to build an agent. Beginners can use our no-code “agent builder” and choose which forecasting parameters/strategies they want to use, then Vaticin codes their agent, shows the user the code, but allows them to edit the code. I hope it will help beginners learn more about coding and AI agents. More experienced builders can connect their own agents through an API. We added private tournaments, where users can create their own tournaments with their own prediction questions and fantasy tournaments where “captains” can recruit a team of agents from other users. Separate leaderboards. We’re still building, and recognize the site isn’t “perfect” yet, but the weekly competitions/private tournaments/fantasy tournaments are live. I’d really appreciate feedback on a few things: - Is Vaticin’s market-based/gamified format different enough from existing forecasting competitions to be relevant? - How would you score and rank agents over the long term? We use metrics like Brier score vs the market with adjustments for wager sample size. What else should we consider? - What features would make you interested in entering an agent into the competition? - Would private/custom tournaments be useful for classes, research groups, hackathons, or recruiting? - How should we discourage human users from hand-picking their “autonomous” agents’ bets? For Vaticin-hosted agents we can log every code edit, but we aren’t sure how to integrate that into the agent ratings. For self-hosted agents we can’t track this at all. Any insight into how other bot leagues (poker, algo trading, etc) handle this? Leaderboard: Note: Early in the competition week, the leaderboard will show many agents at or close to their starting 100,000-token balance because a lot of positions haven't been resolved yet (and tokens are deducted when a wager is made, so the leaderboard will show many agents with less than their initial 100,000 token allocation). Markets: Note: The prediction questions are only visible when the weekly competition cycle is open, so if you visit on the weekend that page may be empty. You can pull up prior weeks’ predictions to take a look. Agent builder: Everything is free right now. No ads. Happy to answer questions. Thanks for any feedback, good or bad. Thanks!

items.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
items.author: kolchinski
items.text: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls. Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call. For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension. For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer. Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. (We’re also benchmarking ThunderPhone on more public benchmarks - stay tuned.) The downside is configuration complexity. Every agent benefits from a different setup on the ThunderPhone stack, and even individual call turns on the same call often benefit from different stacks. Configuring this manually worked for enterprise…

items.text: We all use different agentic systems, bots, chats, and so on. One day I realized that I need to copy context between the apps. It is annoying. So I created a trivial local MCP which sits on top of SQLite and exposes Cypher so LLM can query anything. Also LLM can define a schema if it understands it needs new nodes or edges. How do I use it: 1. I've scanned all my documents and stored passports, driver licences and all kind of contracts for my apartment, insurance and so on. And not only mine - the entire family. 2. I've extracted all the key date and values. Also gemini extracted all the personal relations. Like "Alex is-a-child-of Bob". "Bob is-married-to Anna". So i can ask "give me a passport number of my son" and it gives it back instantly. It might not be a big deal, but it is very convenient. 3. It stores all the projects I'm working on, key steps and decisions. 4. And the most important thing - it works from anywhere. I can ask Hermes i telegram to remind me when my insurance ends or I can reference my project in ClaudeCode just by name and it will get the entire history from Antigravity. I would be happy if you guys find it useful.

items.text: metal : spread the short mat-vec lanes over src1 rows The short mat-vec kernel (K < 32) mapped its 32 lanes to 32 src0 rows and handled one src1 row per threadgroup, so with few src0 rows most lanes were idle. It now covers min(ne01, 32) src0 rows of 32/that src1 rows. This is the weighted sum over the depth states of Inkling 2 since #32855 (1-3 src0 rows, K = number of states, 2304 src1 rows). Inkling-2-Mini UD-Q4_K_XL, M5 Max, master -> this PR: pp512 888 -> 1052 t/s, pp2048 771 -> 894 t/s, tg128 unchanged. PPL and greedy output bit-identical, the graph is unchanged. Tested: test-backend-ops -b MTL0 -o MUL_MAT (new small-K cases). cont : clean-up comment

items.title: huggingface/transformers Release v5.24.0
items.author: Cyrilvallez
items.text: Release v5.24.0 New Model additions Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint (TML-d24-varloop-research) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. Links: Documentation | Blog Post | HF Blog Post Add Inkling2 Mini (#51050) by @guarin Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. It extends the Apertus language model with the EMU3.5 vision tokenizer for images and WavTokenizer for audio. The EMU3.5 tokenizer is an image-only VQGAN with the same encoder as Chameleon's, and it assigns codes by the largest inner product with the codebook. The media tokenizers turn images and audio into discrete tokens, which the language backbone processes alongside text in a shared input vocabulary. The output vocabulary contains only text tokens, so image and audio generation are not supported. Links: Documentation Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft WavTokenizer WavTokenizer encodes 24 kHz mono audio into discrete tokens using a single codebook, at 40 or 75 tokens per second depending on the checkpoint, and reconstructs audio from those tokens. WavTokenizerModel encodes and decodes, and WavTokenizerEncoderModel only encodes. Speech, music/audio and unified checkpoints are available. The 40-token-per-second variant is the audio tokenizer of Apertus 1.5. Training the codec is not supported. Links: Documentation | Paper Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft Dory Dory is a looped (latent-recurrent) language model from NVIDIA. It uses a normalized-GPT architecture with interleaved sliding-window and full attention layers. A shared block of layers is applied repeatedly, so Dory can spend more compute per token. The loop count can be changed at inference time on the same checkpoint to trade speed against quality. Links: Documentation | Paper (nGPT) Add Dory model support (#50099) by @shan18 HY4-VL HY4-VL (Hunyuan V4 Vision-Language) combines the HYV4 mixture-of-experts text backbone with a vision encoder for image-text and video-text generation. It supports dynamic-resolution visual inputs and uses multimodal rotary position embeddings (mRoPE) to represent temporal and spatial positions. It builds on the Qwen2-VL design and shares its vision patch merger with HunYuan-VL. Links: Documentation Add HY4-VL (#50877) by @vasqu Omnilingual ASR Omnilingual ASR is a suite of multilingual speech-recognition models from Meta FAIR that covers more than 1,600 languages. Each model pairs a Wav2Vec2-style audio encoder with one of two heads: CTC (OmniASRForCTC): a linear projection to the vocabulary, decoded non-autoregressively with greedy CTC. Audio language model (OmniASRForConditionalGeneration): audio embeddings are projected into a Llama decoder that generates the transcription. It optionally takes a language code (e.g. "eng_Latn"), which generally improves transcription quality. Both variants come in 300M, 1B, 3B and 7B sizes. Links: Documentation | CTC Documentation | Paper Adding Omnilingual ASR models (#43265) by @ebezzam Lara Mini Lara Mini is a multilingual base language model from Translated with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters per token. It is a hybrid of…

items.author: github-actions[bot]
items.text: model : add hy_v4_flash on the DSA iSWA cache (#32960) model : add hy_v4_flash on the DSA iSWA cache Tencent Hy4 flash is a hy_v4 trunk (iHC, gated MLA, sinks) with sparse and sliding-window MLA layers, sandwich norms, latent routed experts and deepseek41 Engram tables. The sparse layers select their context with a pooled indexer: the keys of 4 consecutive tokens are pooled by a per-channel softmax of a gate plus a position bias, normed, and rotated at the position of the first token. A token attends to the best scored pools of its sequence plus its own pool. The model runs on llama_kv_cache_dsa_iswa as dots3note does. The indexer cache holds the projected value and gate of each token, and the pools are rebuilt from the cells for every ubatch by llama_kv_cache::set_input_kpool(), so there is no pooled state to keep in sync with sequence edits, checkpoints or state save/restore. The selection goes through ggml_top_k_mask with the pool members as blocks and the token's own pool as extra cells. Not covered yet: the MTP block (its tensors are skipped), the vision tower, multiple KV streams, and backends without GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK. convert : add hy_v4_flash The converter of the hy_v4_flash model, without the vision parts. The four Engram tables are written as one per_layer_token_embd tensor of about 127 GB in BF16. Concatenating them with torch.cat materializes the whole tensor at write time, so they are streamed one table at a time in row chunks through the _StreamedBytes path of deepseek41, which keeps the conversion within 100 GB of RAM. tests : add hy_v4_flash to test-llama-archs A 4 layer fixture that alternates sparse and sliding-window layers, with hyper-connections, one Engram module, an indexer on the sparse layers and a latent width distinct from the expert width, so that a transposed routed_down or routed_up is caught. kv-cache : do not shift the pooled indexer cache The pooled indexer of hy_v4_flash caches the value and the gate of each token, without a position: the pooled key is rotated in the graph. A K-shift rotated these rows as if they were roped keys, which broke the pooled keys after a context shift. tests : add the hy_v4_flash Metal fusion baseline model, mtmd : add hy_v4_flash vision The vision tower of hy_v4_flash, with its projector in mtmd and its converter. The published files carry M-RoPE sections, so the text model runs the interleaved M-RoPE path: the rope rows keep their reference order and are reordered to NeoX halves in the graph. The tokens of an image share their position, so the indexer pools now group consecutive tokens in sequence order instead of consecutive positions, and a pooled key is rotated at the four positions of its first member. Without a backend that runs GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK, the picked pools are expanded to their cells and go through build_top_k_mask. CUDA: lightning indexer for 16 heads hy_v4_flash scores its pools with 16 indexer heads, which the CUDA backend did not support, so the scheduler ran the 12 sparse layers' indexers on the CPU at every step. Both kernels already handle 16 heads: the mma kernel needs a multiple of 16 and the vector kernel splits the heads in 4 passes. model : move the Hy4 flash Engram gathers before the token embeddings With the gathers after build_inp_embd, the mixed embedding DUP and SET_ROWS sat between two host nodes and stayed on the CPU. Those ops use every thread, so all the CPU workers woke up on each decoded token for a 12K copy. Gathering first lets the scheduler put them on the GPU, as in qwen4exp, and leaves only small single threaded lookups on the host. llama : speed up the Hy4 flash pool inputs on long contexts set_input_kpool deduplicated the pools through a map keyed by vectors even with a single sequence, sorted cells that are already in order and scanned every pool owner for each token. Dedup only when the ubatch has several sequences, skip the sort when the cells are ordered and mark the earlier pools of the token's sequence…

items.text: ggml-openvino: fix CI op tests and improve KV cache decode (#33002) ggml-openvino: write back consumed in-place nodes of op-test graphs On the naive path every node of an op-test graph is a model output, except an in-place node that another node reads: it got no output, so its destination buffer was never written. GATED_DELTA_NET_CACHE_FUSION copies the final state into the cache and then reads the copy, so the cache kept its old contents. Write such a node back through its view_src, as is already done when nothing reads it. Model graphs are unchanged. ggml-openvino: keep the rest of the buffer in a partial in-place FILL An in-place FILL on a view into part of a larger buffer produced only the filled values. Its output stands for the whole in-place source, so the write-back put those values at the start of the buffer and not at the view's offset. For a contiguous view with a static shape, build the whole buffer: the elements before the view, the filled values, then the elements after it. Add NodeContext::get_inplace_op_src() to detect the in-place case. ggml-openvino: fix softplus precision for large negative inputs softplus was computed as relu(x) + log(1 + exp(-|x|)). When exp(-|x|) is below the precision of 1 + exp(-|x|), the log returns 0 or one ulp, so for x below about -16 in f32 the result was 0 or far off. The SOFTPLUS test case with inputs in [-16.6, -16] fails on CPU and GPU. Compute log1p(y) for y = exp(-|x|) with the series y - y^2/2 + y^3/3 - y^4/4 when y < 0.01, where its relative error is below 2e-9, and keep log(1 + y) above that. ggml-openvino: finer GPU KV rounding for decode batches Rounding the GPU KV length up to a power of two makes a batch attend up to twice the rows that hold data right after each power of two. Decode reads every attended row, so long contexts lose decode speed. The GPU plugin keeps memory for each attended length: several large buffers for a prompt batch, about one copy of K and V for a decode batch. Keep the power of two for prompt batches (more than 16 tokens per sequence), and round decode batches up to a multiple of 2^k / 4 and of 256. That is four lengths per power of two, with at most 25% masked rows. ggml-openvino : keep the head axis of the 4-D KV cache static ggml-openvino: split two one-line lambdas per clang-format The backend's .clang-format keeps a lambda on one line only when it is a function argument (AllowShortLambdasOnASingleLine: Inline). The constant helpers in the softplus and FILL translators are assigned to variables, so clang-format splits them. Formatting only. items.title: DyLoMo-DiT: Dynamic Looped Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Transformers
items.author: Lernie Li, Yuanliu Liu, Pengfei Xiong
items.text: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. On ImageNet 256times256, DyLoMo-DiT reduces FID by 11-24% relative to DiT and 36-56% relative to DiT-MoE at matched parameter and compute budgets. For text-to-image generation, a scaled DyLoMo-DiT achieves a higher GenEval score than FLUX.1 (0.714 vs. 0.673), with less than one tenth of its active parameters (1.05B vs. 12B).

items.title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
items.author: Xingjian Ran, Xiaoye Mo, Sihao Liu
items.text: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

items.title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
items.author: Feixiang Ruan, Guodong Lv, Kewei Zhang
items.text: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

items.title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
items.author: Zeyang Guan, Qihao Zhao, Rui Gong
items.text: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where a retained procedure applies, it acts without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEK's average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests.

items.text: server : handle CTRL_BREAK_EVENT on Windows for clean shutdown (#32080) Windows can't send SIGINT to a child process, so scripts that launch llama-server could only kill it, which skips the clean shutdown. On other platforms, stop it with SIGINT. In both cases, kill it afterwards as a fallback. tests: add test_server_ctrl_break (Windows only) and a ServerProcess.share_console option. Console control events only reach a server that shares the test's console, hence the option. items.text: ggml: allow input async copies (#30685) ggml: allow input async copies Copy the host inputs of a split with set_tensor_async followed by a single synchronize, instead of one blocking copy per input. This is opt-in per device through the new async_host_input cap, which only CUDA sets. Other backends keep the current path. The async path is used without pipeline parallelism only. With pipeline parallelism, the input backend also waits on the slot event before an async copy, since CUDA peer copies run on the source stream. items.title: SoundWeaver: Compositional Warm-Starting for Text-to-Audio Diffusion Serving
items.author: Ayush Barik, Sofia Stoica, Nikhil Sarda, Arnav Kethana, Abhinav Khanduja, Muchen Xu, Fan Lai
items.text: Text-to-audio (T2A) diffusion models generate high-quality audio but require tens of neural function evaluations (NFEs), resulting in substantial inference latency. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize each generation trajectory independently, even when reusable acoustic structure exists in prior examples. We introduce SoundWeaver, the first training-free framework for compositional cross example acoustic reuse. Rather than generating from pure noise, SoundWeaver constructs a prompt-conditioned acoustic prior from segments distributed across cached audios and warm-starts diffusion from an intermediate noise level. We introduce an Acoustic Composition Graph (ACG), which uses neural codec representations and segment-level identification to identify candidate cross-cache transitions and structured path search to jointly optimize prompt relevance and acoustic continuity. We further establish a warm-start error bound showing how prior quality and diffusion SNR jointly govern the admissible skip depth, motivating an adaptive contextual-bandit Skip Gater that selects the warm-start level for each request. Across T2A diffusion backbones, SoundWeaver achieves 1.48-3.74x generation speedup with only a 1K-clip cache while improving generation quality.

items.title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
items.author: Vaishak Girish Kumar, Sanika Vilas Najan
items.text: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.

items.title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
items.author: Jiaming Liu, Fenlou Zhai, Ao Xue, Liangliang Tang, Cheng Ding, Daoqiang Zhang
items.text: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope combines shared multiscale pressure encoding, learned scale fusion and sensor-probability averaging, allowing measurement sets to change without retraining. Separate models evaluate unstart detection and new-onset prediction within a 0.5-s future interval. Seven Mach-2.9 runs, each with one annotated event, cover downstream throttling, throat regulation and splitter adjustment; three are held out with fixed weights and source-derived settings. Across three training seeds, full-sensor detection achieves run-wise mean window $F_1$ scores of 0.834--0.964. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces detection-score variation across sensor subsets in both splitter runs while retaining mean scores close to those of the full sets. Regional detection favors cowl and high-speed-channel measurements during splitter adjustment and compression-side measurements during downstream throttling, consistent with their respective pressure responses. Complete-record evaluation shows that configurations with comparable window scores can produce different alarm timing and persistence. These findings connect sensor count and regional coverage to pressure discrimination and sequential alarm behavior, providing experimental guidance for configuring inlet monitoring systems.

items.title: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios
items.author: Jie Peng, Davis Hobley, Song Wang, Zachary PlotkinB, Tianlong Chen
items.text: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.

items.title: Validation Bias in Large Language Model Responses to Cancer Treatment Queries: A Factorial Cross-Sectional Study
items.author: Ramez Kouzy, Saketh Vinjamuri, Sarah Ghalayini, Jack Gallifant, Shan Chen, Marielle Fis Loperana, Roxanna Attar-Olyaee, Danielle S. Bitterman
items.text: Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used by patients seeking cancer information, but their safety when users present evidence-misaligned beliefs about treatment remains uncharacterized. We hypothesized that LLMs exhibit validation bias, affirming rather than correcting such beliefs, and evaluated this with a 2x2x2 factorial design crossing conversation format (single-turn vs multi-turn), treatment type (evidence-based vs alternative), and query valence (positive vs negative). Framing was evidence-aligned (supporting evidence-based treatments or questioning alternative therapies) or evidence-misaligned (promoting alternative treatments or questioning evidence-based therapies). We analyzed 1,272 conversations (6,360 interactions) across 14 LLMs from 6 vendors, scored by an LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) validated against human annotation on a 6-dimension safety rubric. The primary outcome was the unsafe response rate, defined as a Weak classification or any critical failure. Evidence-misaligned framing increased unsafe response rates compared with evidence-aligned framing (14.4% vs 5.1%; OR 3.14, 95% CI 2.07-4.78; P < .001), and the association persisted after accounting for clustering by LLM. Among 429 conversations classified as Strong under evidence-aligned framing, 22.6% were downgraded in their paired evidence-misaligned counterpart. Multi-turn conversations had lower unsafe response rates than single-turn conversations (5.2% vs 14.7%; P < .001). Unsafe response rates varied by vendor from 1.8% to 36.8%. LLMs exhibited significant validation bias in oncology, with unsafe responses nearly tripling under evidence-misaligned framing. Evaluations limited to neutral, fact-seeking queries may overestimate real-world safety, and safety testing of medical AI systems should include evidence-misaligned user framing.

items.title: DAGGER: Deployment-Free Quality Estimation for Generative AI Workflows
items.author: Dimitrios Liakopoulos, Neeraja J. Yadwadkar
items.text: Estimating the quality of generative AI workflows is challenging because these workflows comprise multiple stages, and errors can propagate across them, making end-to-end performance depend not only on the accuracy of individual models but also on how their outputs affect downstream stages. Each stage can use one of many candidate models. Estimating end-to-end workflow quality by deploying and evaluating every resulting model configuration is therefore prohibitively expensive. As a result, existing approaches face a tradeoff between estimation cost and accuracy: inexpensive methods often produce unreliable quality estimates, while accurate methods require deploying and evaluating many workflow configurations. In this paper, we introduce DAGGER, a framework for estimating the quality of generative AI workflows without exhaustive deployment and profiling. DAGGER represents a workflow as a graph, in which nodes correspond to stages and edges capture how outputs from one stage affect subsequent stages. It then decomposes workflow quality into per-node accuracy terms and per-edge dependency terms. Using a novel analytical formulation and SVD-based matrix completion, DAGGER estimates workflow quality from sparse observations without executing every candidate workflow. We evaluate DAGGER on three generative AI workflows across three datasets. DAGGER estimates workflow quality with a median error of 6.8 percentage points while reducing profiling cost by 10.2$\times$ relative to BenchPress, a state-of-the-art baseline, and selects workflow configurations competitive with state-of-the-art frameworks such as LLMSelector.

items.title: Instantiation of Human Values in Image Generation
items.author: Maria-Teresa De Rosa Palmini, Piera Riccio, Noa Garcia, Eva Cetinic
items.text: Text-to-image (T2I) models are increasingly embedded in everyday visual culture, yet little is known about how they translate abstract human values into visual scenes. We address this gap by introducing a framework, grounded in Schwartz's theory of basic human values, for studying value instantiation: the process by which ideals such as success, care, or freedom are visually realized. Using person-centered prompts from 70 positive and negative value items, we generate 28,000 images across four state-of-the-art T2I models. We identify visual prototypes, recurring combinations of subjects, actions, and settings, and use them to quantify how narrowly models instantiate these values and how this breadth compares with human descriptions of the same items. We then map these prototypes onto a taxonomy of social configurations spanning setting, sociality, mode of engagement, and social register, revealing what is systematically foregrounded or omitted. Our results show that T2I models produce far more concentrated representations than humans do when describing the same values. They default to a hyper-individualistic, adult-centric worldview, reproducing value-specific associations, such as achievement tied to formal institutional settings or hedonism rendered as affluent consumption, while marginalizing everyday labor, relational care, and non-adult perspectives. As a proof of concept, we show that these structural gaps can guide a steering method that diversifies outputs without modifying the original prompt.

items.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
items.author: Noureldin Zahran, Mohammed E. Fouda, Khaled N. Khasawneh
items.text: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.

items.title: INCLUDE-2.0: Disentangling Knowledge Gaps in Multilingual LLM Evaluation
items.author: Angelika Romanou, Maria Grandury, Clara Meister, Negar Foroutan, Jabez Magomere, Anna Sotnikova, Hitesh Laxmichand Patel, Akshay Kumar Dubey, Alfonso Amayuelas, Amit Agarwal, Arion Das, Carlos…
items.text: Current multilingual benchmarks cover only a fraction of the languages represented in modern pretraining corpora and often conflate language proficiency with the ability to answer questions grounded in specific regions and communities. We introduce INCLUDE-2.0, a large-scale benchmark for region-aware multilingual factual evaluation, which covers 91 languages from 86 countries (127 total language--country pairs), comprising over 220K curated samples drawn from native regional sources. Unlike existing benchmarks that often treat language as a proxy for region, IINCLUDE-2.0 distinguishes between questions whose answers are independent of context, vary by country, concern widely documented facts about a place, or depend on knowledge primarily expressed through local linguistic and cultural sources. Each item is annotated with its regional knowledge type and domain, and paired with an English translation, enabling controlled analysis of the relationship between language proficiency and possession of regional knowledge. Evaluating frontier and open-weight models on IINCLUDE-2.0, we find that aggregate multilingual accuracy masks substantial variation across regional knowledge types, languages, and regions. We find that frontier models perform worse on locally embedded knowledge than on widely documented facts about regions, with an average drop of ~14.5 points. We also show that for open-weight models, scale improves accuracy but does not reliably make performance invariant to whether a question is asked in English or its original language. INCLUDE-2.0 is available at

items.title: Directly Maximizing On-policy Expected Accepted Length for Speculative Decoding
items.author: Ziying Zhang, Yaqing Wang, Yong Liu, Quanming Yao
items.text: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose tokens for verification by a target model. Draft training commonly optimizes token-level distribution alignment, but this does not directly optimize the length of the accepted prefix: once a draft token is rejected, all subsequent draft tokens are discarded. We propose FreDraft, an on-policy training method that directly maximizes the expected accepted length of drafts sampled from the current draft model. This objective accounts for first-rejection truncation and induces prefix-aware credit assignment, weighting each token by its contribution to the acceptance of the current and subsequent tokens. To optimize the objective efficiently, we analytically marginalize token-level acceptance rate, using the target model's vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance. We further redistribute part of this distribution-level gradient into an explicit penalty for sampled tokens whose probabilities are overestimated by the draft model, while preserving the expected gradient. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models show that FreDraft improves accepted length and decoding speedup over strong baselines, achieving faster on-policy training convergence.

items.title: scOPD: Routed On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM-Based Single-Cell Annotation
items.author: Zhiyin Yu, Yuchen Mou, Songtao Huang, Shuaiyu Zhang, Xing Wei, Chunchun Chen, Wei Ye, Xiao Luo, Zhonghai Wu, Xiangchao Yan, Lei Bai, Shiyang Feng, Bo Zhang
items.text: Motivation: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for single-cell annotation, but existing training methods mainly rely on scalar outcome rewards that provide limited supervision for intermediate biological reasoning. Batch-level annotation is particularly challenging because it requires jointly resolving local cell identities and a global one-to-one matching constraint, such that one local error can affect the entire assignment. Moreover, a single inference pass provides insufficient evidence for locating uncertain predictions. These limitations call for fine-grained reasoning supervision during training and uncertainty-aware refinement during inference. Results: To address these challenges, we propose scOPD, an on-policy self-distillation framework for LLM-based single-cell annotation. After reasoning fine-tuning, scOPD adaptively routes qualified rollouts to reward-based optimization, while erroneous rollouts receive privileged token-level supervision from successful sibling trajectories. During inference, rollout disagreement triggers constraint-aware pairwise refinement of uncertain assignments. Across CellPuzzles and four out-of-domain disease datasets, scOPD consistently improves the performance of diverse LLM backbones, achieving average cell-level and batch-level accuracies of 81.71% and 44.49% with Qwen3-8B. Availability and Implementation: Code and data are available at

items.title: RECAP: Training Long-horizon LLM Agents with Context Compaction
items.author: Yulun Jiang, Maria Brbic, Michael Moor
items.text: Context compaction enables large language model agents to tackle long-horizon tasks within limited context budgets by replacing interaction histories with compressed summaries. However, learning effective compaction jointly with the agent policy remains challenging, as summaries affect task success over many subsequent interactions. We introduce RECAP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. We show that the gradient of the distortion objective decomposes into two complementary learning signals: distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. Experiments on Qwen3.5-4B show that RECAP consistently outperforms the task-reward-only RL baselines on both environments, leading to an absolute improvement of 4.6% and 4.3% on BrowseComp-plus and SWE-bench Verified, respectively. Ablations further highlight the value of jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior for RECAP.

items.title: RecipeADQA: A User-aware Question-Answering Dataset for Multi-Constraint Recipe Recommendation
items.author: Haotian Li, Shuai Jiang, Sayaka Kamei, Yasuhiko Morimoto
items.text: Question-answering recipe recommendation tasks lack datasets with ground-truth labels. Existing methods often generate datasets from simple combinations of ingredient or tag constraints, leading to unnatural expressions and unreasonable constraints that are hard to reflect users' real preferences. This paper proposes a construction method for a benchmark-style QA dataset for natural-language recipe recommendation. Driven by real user behavior, our method integrates external user query and review data to extract fine-grained preference signals by LLMs and maps them onto a knowledge-graph-based tag schema, thereby constructing QA data consisting of preference and ingredient constraints. Besides, a greedy strategy for constraint selection is also used to control the answer size, while tag-based re-ranking is applied to improve data quality. The generated dataset RecipeADQA contains natural-language questions, structured constraints, and answer sets, resulting in 128,465 instances. Experiments compare RecipeADQA with baseline datasets from two perspectives: data quality and retrieval-recommendation performance. The results show that ours outperforms existing methods on the same recipe knowledge graph in coverage, higher question quality in naturalness and constraint rationality, and better queryability. Moreover, we design a noise-augmented retrieve-and-rerank model, in which a lightweight parser first retrieves candidate recipes, and a small language model then selects and ranks relevant recipes from a noisy candidate pool. The model trained on RecipeADQA outperforms the same model trained on the baseline datasets. The relevant construction code and data have been open-sourced at a GitHub repository

items.title: Capability and Interpretability of Transformers on Multi-task Recurrence
items.author: Xiamin Chen, Linyu Liu, Jiachen Hu, Pinyan Lu
items.text: Transformers are widely used in various language tasks, with limited understanding of their internal mechanisms. Motivated by the recurrent structure of many linguistic rules, we study the capability and interpretability of Transformers through a controlled family of linear recurrence tasks over finite cyclic groups. These tasks range from executing a single fixed rule to identifying a latent rule from context and switching between explicitly specified rules, with and without input masking. Through extensive experiments across different configurations, we find that switching specified rules is simpler than identifying latent rules for Transformers in general. We also identify how several key factors affect the generalization capability of Transformers, including the depth, width, and the algebraic structure of the linear recurrence. Curriculum training is extremely useful when the number of rules is large. With standard tools in mechanistic interpretability like linear probing and input patching, our study reveals how Transformers represent, identify, and execute multiple rules.

items.title: Does Item Response Theory Generalize Across Languages? Evidence from Cross-Lingual LLM Benchmarks
items.author: Ruchira Dhar, Qiwei Peng, Anders S{\o}gaard
items.text: The application of Item Response Theory (IRT) for data selection in benchmarks has mostly been limited to monolingual settings. In this work, we ask: how does IRT generalize when the same benchmark is translated across languages? We conduct experiments on Multilingual GSM and Global MMLU, covering over 100 language models and 11 languages. Fitting 1PL, 2PL, and 3PL IRT models per language, we assess cross-lingual consistency of parameters and whether IRT-filtered subsets preserve model rankings across languages: item difficulty emerges as the most stable parameter followed by guessing and then discrimination. A differential item analysis also shows that lack of stability can be tracked to specific items shifting under translation across languages. Our findings suggest IRT-based selection in multilingual settings must be both parameter-aware and item-aware, validating model choice and screening individual items before assuming cross-lingual generalization.

items.title: RegioZH: Unveiling Comprehension Disparities across Regional Chinese Varieties in LLMs
items.author: Weihua Zheng, Wu Kui, Thong T. Doan, Lin Jingxia, AiTi Aw, Nancy F. Chen, Roy Ka-Wei Lee
items.text: Current evaluations often treat Chinese varieties as monolithic, obscuring failures for regional users. We introduce RegioZH, a 2,607-item multiple-choice benchmark for regional lexical reasoning across Mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia. Built by region-specific annotators and expert-validated, it targets localized idioms, slang, code-mixing, politeness conventions, and sociocultural expressions. Zero-shot results on eleven LLMs show large disparities, including a 29.4-point average accuracy gap between Taiwan and Singapore. Persona and structured chain-of-thought prompts for five models yield selective gains, suggesting that some errors stem from retrieval or framing rather than only missing knowledge. Representation, attention, calibration, and surface-feature analyses show a dissociation between marker attention and semantic grounding, overconfident forced-choice errors, and localized lexical density as a consistent difficulty predictor. Qualitative analysis finds terminology misunderstandings, sociocultural inference gaps, and cross-regional semantic divergence. RegioZH demonstrates that apparent Chinese proficiency can mask uneven understanding across regional varieties, motivating intra-language robustness evaluation alongside multilingual generalization.

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Iranian Doctoral Entrance Exams in Electrical and Computer Engineering
items.author: Sima Akbari Neisiyani, Hossein Taghizad
items.text: We evaluate four large language models (LLMs) on multiple-choice questions from the 2024 and 2025 Iranian national Ph.D. entrance examinations in Electrical Engineering (EE) and Computer Engineering (CE). Of the 440 questions in the four official booklets, 7 were excluded because the question statement or its figure was ambiguous, leaving 433 questions (186 EE, 247 CE), of which 171 (39.5\%) depend on a figure. Each question was presented in the original Persian and in an English translation, giving 3,464 scored responses. GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Grok 4 were queried zero-shot, with reasoning enabled, through a single commercial web interface (Perplexity) in October 2025, using an automated script. Because every model answers the same items, all inferences use paired tests or question-clustered models. Accuracy separates into two tiers: GPT-5 (79.9\%, 95\% CI 76.6--83.1) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (78.4\%, 74.8--81.9) are statistically indistinguishable, and both outperform Grok 4 (71.7\%) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (71.3\%) by 6.7--8.7 percentage points (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$). The English--Persian accuracy difference is small for every model ($-0.2$ to $+2.5$ points; exact McNemar $p \ge 0.28$). For three models the 90\% confidence interval lies within $\pm 5$ points, so differences larger than this can be excluded. Questions with figures are much harder: the odds ratio is 0.30 (95\% CI 0.21--0.43) after adjusting for discipline. The apparent EE deficit of two models disappears once the larger share of figure-based EE items is accounted for. We describe the dataset, the protocol and its limitations, including the uncontrolled web-retrieval and decoding settings of the interface, and release item-level responses and analysis code.

items.title: How Persona Conditioning Changes Open-Ended Task Execution: A Paired Evaluation of Behavioral Gains and Reliability Costs
items.author: Yugyeong Ji, Changho Lee, Yerin Hwang, Taegwan Kang, Jinsik Lee
items.text: Large language models (LLMs) are often prompted with role- or persona-based instructions, yet persona conditioning has mainly been evaluated through character fidelity or aggregate benchmark accuracy. We study persona conditioning as a task-execution steering signal that changes how models interpret, structure, and sustain responses. Using paired instances derived from real user role-play logs and expanded into simulated multi-turn continuations, we compare with-persona and no-persona conditions while fixing task content, constraints, user simulation, and evaluation criteria. Across eight models, persona conditioning improves expert content depth and procedural fidelity, and these gains survive length control. At the same time, it lowers strict instruction-following accuracy by 17 to 30 points in every model evaluated, and increases unsupported real-world specificity through persona-induced elaboration. These results suggest that persona prompting is not a general-purpose performance improvement technique, but a selective task-execution policy shift with both behavioral gains and reliability risks.

items.title: SD-Cache: Learnable Memory Consolidation with State-Guided Dynamic Caching
items.author: Yuanhong Chen, Yiping Ji, Cameron Gordon, Emily Hackett-Jones, Hemanth Saratchandran, Anton van den Hengel
items.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as persistent services that must reason over large volumes of external knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model responses in relevant documents, but the retrieved content must still be encoded and stored in the key-value (KV) cache. As this content accumulates, the cache grows linearly, increasing memory consumption and inference cost. Existing memory-compression methods address this problem either by retaining a subset of cached states or by learning context compressors that map documents to compact latent representations. Despite these advances, consolidating information under tight memory budgets while preserving its usefulness for future queries remains challenging. We investigate how the model's native KV states can be selectively consolidated into a fixed-size working memory without access to future queries. To this end, we introduce SD-Cache (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache), a query-agnostic KV-memory consolidation framework that operates alongside a frozen generator LLM. SD-Cache learns to consolidate layer-wise KV states into fixed-size memory through selective anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, processing new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimisation. Experiments on retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks show that SD-Cache maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets.

items.title: AhaPro: A Process-level Rebus benchmark for probing Aha moments in LLM reasoning
items.author: Wei Guo, Lang Qin, Yundi Gai, Qinghua Xu, Zhi Wu, Wenjian Ding, Huijia Li, Zhenglu Yang, Yao Zhang
items.text: Existing research on Aha moments in large language models has largely focused on reflective expressions or final revision outcomes, leaving their role in the visible reasoning process insufficiently characterized. Rebus puzzles encode answers through character forms, spatial arrangements, and homophony. Reinterpreting key details may trigger Aha moments and shifts in the reasoning process and candidate answers. We introduce AhaPro, a process-level benchmark that uses rebus puzzles to examine how models reorganize evidence and revise answers through Aha moments. The framework represents CoT as sequences of candidate answers, evidence, and verification states, using hierarchical metrics to assess conflict detection, state improvement, and subsequent adoption. Across eleven models, we observe frequent failures to adopt better states discovered during Aha moments, alongside adopted revisions that leave state quality unchanged or reduce it. Models also detect conflicts without subsequently achieving an effective revision. Further paired interventions suggest that prior reasoning context may hinder effective revision after conflict detection, while multi-branch search highlights answer selection as a bottleneck between correct-answer discovery and successful correction.

items.title: Reliability of Language-Model Judges for Quantitative Scientific Question Answering: Evidence from Perovskite Photovoltaics
items.author: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou, Gaoxiang Yuan
items.text: Evaluating retrieval-augmented language models increasingly relies on automated model judges, yet their reliability on quantitative scientific synthesis remains largely unmeasured. Here, we evaluate automated grading on a quantitative benchmark for perovskite photovoltaics, where all 755 ground-truth answers are deterministically computed from 45,441 experimental device records. We evaluate a frontier judge (Claude Opus 5.5) alongside two local open-weight judges (Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-8B) across 4,530 free-text answers from six retrieval architectures under three regimes: reference-augmented (with the computed key), evidence-augmented (with retrieved passages and query logs), and unassisted (question and answer alone). Equipped with the reference key, Claude Opus reproduces ground truth near-perfectly (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.982 \pm 0.003$) and preserves exact architectural rankings ($\tau = 1.00$). Withholding the reference causes evaluation fidelity to collapse: frontier agreement drops to $\kappa = 0.557 \pm 0.022$, and providing retrieved literature passages yields virtually no improvement ($\kappa = 0.576 \pm 0.024$). Without reference keys, local judges degrade to near-random agreement ($\kappa = 0.087$ and $0.112$), inverting the leaderboard to rank a hallucinating closed-book baseline first ($\tau \le 0.20$). Furthermore, SQL-augmented generations induce severe evaluative blind spots: absent a reference, the frontier judge accepts 46.6% of erroneous SQL answers, overestimating architecture accuracy as 66.4% against its true 52.6%. These findings demonstrate that model-based evaluation in the physical sciences cannot rely on unstructured text inspection; rigorous benchmarking requires reference ground truth precomputed from structured measurement records.

items.title: Agentic Optimization: LLM Agents Select and Configure Algorithms for Engineering Design
items.author: Dominic Mashak, Jacob Schrum
items.text: Engineers solving new multi-objective design problems commonly commit to a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) before seeing a result. The best MOEA differs from benchmark to benchmark. We propose agentic optimization, placing an LLM agent outside the optimization loop, where it reads a natural-language problem description to configure and launch algorithms, drawing on parametric knowledge rather than on a performance history that a novel problem lacks. We compare five LLMs in a fixed harness on four engineering benchmarks and a real-world SARS-CoV-2 molecular docking task, using hypervolume (HV) and IGD+ with multiple comparison-corrected tests. Three models (GPT, DeepSeek, Qwen) dominate every baseline on combined HV and IGD+, and each is significantly better than the best baseline on at least one benchmark, sometimes by applying the same baseline algorithm they surpass, showing the importance of both algorithm configuration and selection. Agent behavior is strongly model-dependent, but even the weakest agents dominate three of the four baselines overall.

items.title: LLM Genetic Feature Engineering
items.author: Jonathan Thompson, Razvan Stefanescu, Manoj Varma Namburi, Liuxia Wang
items.text: Feature Engineering is the (traditionally manual) process of constructing derived variables from an existing dataset by combining, transforming, or otherwise manipulating the original data fields to reduce statistical noise and extract meaningful, domain-specific quantities of interest from the raw dataset. Recent work demonstrates promising progress toward the au tomation of this process through the integration of large language models (LLMs) and various metaheuristics to guide the search for useful features. We build on this approach by introducing a novel genetic algorithm that implements selection, crossover, and mutation at the individual feature level, rather than at the level of the entire engineered feature set. In doing so, we enable in-process statistical analysis of newly-generated features, thereby enabling the genetic algorithm to simultaneously integrate individual and group-level feature metrics into its selec tion process. We demonstrate this capability using state-of-the-art feature importance metrics, and show that this approach yields superior predictive performance while driving meaningful improvements in feature relevance, algorithm robustness, and overall model interpretability.

items.title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
items.author: Marcelo Fernandez
items.text: Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act. In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties. We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation). Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these dimensions without loss of correctness or stability. Allocation, in particular, acts as a first-class constraint that prevents simplification of the governance stack. We validate these results through a series of analytical constructions and empirical ablations, showing that removing or approximating any layer leads to systematic failure modes. This work reframes agent governance as a structural problem: not only how actions are executed, but how access to execution is determined, and why these decisions impose irreducible architectural requirements.

items.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
items.author: Richard DeMillo, Richard Lipton
items.text: Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts. The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.

items.title: PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL: Polarization-Keyed Examination Papers and Mandatory Issued Eyewear that Displace AI Glasses and Extend Universal Design
items.author: Dohyeon Kwon
items.text: Camera-equipped AI glasses turn an examination page into a query for a remote vision-language model. Device detection targets possession, and our companion work SEOYUN targets the model. PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL instead changes who owns the eyewear. Every candidate wears authority-issued glasses for the whole session, and the question paper is printed so that it can be read only through them. As in cinema stereoscopy, a patterned laminate encodes the text in the handedness of circular polarization rather than in brightness. The page looks uniformly grey to the naked eye and to unfiltered cameras, and the issued circular analyzer reveals the text. Compulsory issued eyewear turns the smart-glasses form factor against itself. The face position is occupied by a device the authority supplies and collects, and a camera anywhere else needs its own analyzer. Spectacle wearers receive prescription inserts in the issued frame, low-vision candidates may use an offline assistive mixed-reality tier, and blind candidates keep braille, audio, and screen-reader formats. We derive the luminance and contrast budget and show why circular keying tolerates head tilt. A simulation study supports the analysis. A spectral Mueller model confirms tilt invariance and invisibility to linear-polarization cameras, but a 1 degree axis misregistration leaks a few percent of contrast. A capture-and-OCR experiment on English and Korean text shows that video averaging can recover leakage too weak to read in a single frame, so leakage must be bounded against the adversary's total photon budget. Data from 151 observers and 28 cameras show that spectral (metameric) keys are visible to all of them. The key carries no secrecy, and filtered covert cameras remain possible. All results are simulations; no prototypes, physical measurements, or human-subject results are reported.

items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
items.author: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume
items.text: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts.

items.title: Differential evolution with perturbation for continuous function optimization
items.author: Takuya Muto, Michiharu Maeda
items.text: This paper presents differential evolution with perturbation (DEP) for continuous function optimization. Differential evolution is a simple and efficient algorithm. Perturbation is the phenomenon that the motion by the contribution of the main force is disturbed by the influence subsidiary power.
